Introduction

Financial management centres on three core decision areas: Investment Decisions, Financing Decisions, and Dividend Decisions. This lab is devoted to the first of these — usually called Capital Budgeting — concerned with the optimum utilisation of funds to maximise the wealth of an organisation and, in turn, its shareholders.

Capital budgeting is crucial for an organisation to fulfil its objectives — it generates revenue and ensures the organisation's long-term existence. Even not-for-profit entities must make capital budgeting decisions, though not to earn profit but to fulfil their mission. Because every rupee of capital raised bears a cost (the cost of capital), each rupee raised must be invested prudently — which requires proper planning through a proper budget. That's exactly why these decisions are called Capital Budgeting: applying the principles of budgeting to capital investment.

In simple terms, Capital Budgeting involves: 1. Identification of investment projects that are strategic to the business's overall objectives 2. Estimating and evaluating post-tax incremental cash flows for each investment proposal 3. Selection of an investment proposal that maximises the return to investors

Learning Outcomes of This Lab

  • State the objectives of capital investment decisions.
  • Discuss the importance and purpose of capital budgeting for a business entity.
  • Calculate cash flows in capital budgeting decisions and explain the basic principles for measuring them.
  • Discuss the various investment evaluation techniques — Payback Period, ARR, NPV, PI, IRR, Discounted Payback Period, and MIRR.
  • Apply the concepts of each technique to capital investment decision making.
  • Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each technique.

How This Lab Is Organised

Section 1 — Estimation of Cash Flows→Section 2 — Capital Budgeting Techniques

Every capital budgeting decision ultimately rests on two pillars: getting the cash flow estimate right, and applying the right evaluation technique to it. This lab follows that same two-section structure — first cash flows, then techniques — before finishing with special cases, a summary, and the full question bank.

Purpose of Capital Budgeting

Capital budgeting decisions are important, crucial, and critical business decisions for four reasons:

(i) Substantial Expenditure

Investment decisions fulfil long-term objectives and the very existence of an organisation. A substantial capital investment is required, and the size and timing of cash flows determine which sources of finance are selected — hence the need for thorough study and planning.

(ii) Long Time Period

The effect of a capital budgeting decision plays out over a long period. These decisions affect not just future benefits and costs but also the rate and direction of the firm's growth.

(iii) Irreversibility

Most investment decisions are irreversible — once implemented, it is very difficult, and rarely economically feasible, to reverse them, due to upfront payments, contractual obligations, or technological impossibilities.

(iv) Complex Decisions

Capital investment decisions require assessing future events, which are inherently difficult to predict. It is often equally difficult to estimate, in quantitative terms, all the benefits or costs relating to a particular investment decision.

Capital Budgeting Process

How formalised and systematic the capital budgeting process needs to be depends on the size of the organisation, the number of projects under consideration, the direct financial benefit of each project, the composition of the firm's existing assets and management's desire to change that composition, and the timing of expenditures associated with the projects finally accepted.

1. Planning→2. Evaluation→3. Selection→4. Implementation→5. Control→6. Review
  • Planning — begins with identifying potential investment opportunities; the opportunity is assessed for its potential effect on the firm's fortunes and the management's ability to exploit it. Opportunities with little merit are rejected; promising ones advance to evaluation as a formal proposal.
  • Evaluation — determines the proposal's investments, inflows and outflows. Appraisal techniques ranging from simple payback and ARR to sophisticated discounted cash flow techniques are used. The technique chosen should enable the best decision given prevailing circumstances.
  • Selection — considering the returns and risks of individual projects as well as the organisation's cost of capital, the firm chooses among projects to maximise shareholders' wealth.
  • Implementation — once the final selection is made, the firm acquires the necessary funds, purchases the assets, and begins implementing the project.
  • Control — progress is monitored via feedback reports, including capital expenditure progress reports and performance reports comparing actual performance against plans, plus post-completion audits.
  • Review — when a project terminates (or even before), the organisation reviews it to explain its success or failure — with implications for future planning and evaluation, and ideas for new proposals.

Types of Capital Investment Decisions

Capital investment decisions are generally classified in two ways: on the basis of the firm's existence, and on the basis of the decision situation.

On the Basis of Firm's Existence

New firms need decisions like selecting a plant to install; existing firms need decisions to meet new environments or competitive challenges.

  • Replacement & Modernisation decisions — aim to improve operating efficiency and reduce cost. Plant/machinery requires replacement either because its economic life is over (replacement decision) or because it has become technologically outdated (modernisation decision). Both are called cost reduction decisions.
  • Expansion decisions — existing successful firms experiencing growth in demand, or shortages/delays in delivery due to inadequate production facilities, consider adding capacity to an existing product line.
  • Diversification decisions — evaluating proposals to diversify into new product lines or markets, to reduce the risk of failure by operating across different products or markets.

Both expansion and diversification decisions are called revenue expansion decisions.

On the Basis of Decision Situation

  • Mutually exclusive decisions — accepting one proposal excludes accepting the others (e.g. choosing between a semi-automatic and a highly automatic machine for the same job).
  • Accept-Reject decisions — proposals are independent and don't compete with each other; a proposal is accepted if it clears a minimum required return, and rejected otherwise.
  • Contingent decisions — proposals are dependent on each other; investing in one requires investing in one or more others (e.g. setting up a factory in a remote area requires investing in roads, employee housing, etc.).

Steps of Capital Budgeting Procedure

1. Estimate cash flows over the entire life of each project→2. Evaluate each alternative using different decision criteria→3. Determine the minimum required rate of return (WACC) as the discount rate

This is exactly why this lab is divided into two sections: Estimation of Cash Flows (covered next) and Capital Budgeting Techniques (covered from the Techniques Overview tab onward).

Estimation of Project Cash Flows — Key Considerations

Capital budgeting analysis considers only incremental cash flows likely to result from accepting a project — estimating future cash flows is one of the most important tasks in capital budgeting. Note that Accounting Rate of Return evaluates profitability on the basis of accounting profit, which has limitations: the timing of cash flow may not match the period of profit, and non-cash items like depreciation involve no immediate cash outflow. Cash flows are estimated using inputs from Production, Finance, Marketing and other departments. The project's cash outflows are its costs; its cash inflows are its benefits. The project's life may be determined by technological obsolescence, physical deterioration, and decline in demand for the project's output — uncertainty is always present, however good the firm's forecasting.

(a) Depreciation — the Tax Shield

Depreciation is a non-cash item and does not itself affect cash flow — but its tax shield must be considered, since it reduces the tax cash outflow, and that reduction is itself a cash inflow.

Depreciation Tax Shield Calculator

(b) Opportunity Cost

Opportunity cost is the benefit foregone by choosing an alternative investment option. For example, if a company owns land bought years ago for ₹1 crore that could be sold today for ₹10 crore, and instead uses it for a project, the ₹10 crore sale value forms part of the initial outlay — because by using the land, the company forwent the ₹10 crore it could have earned selling it. Opportunity costs can arise both at the initial outlay and during the project's tenure, and are considered part of cash outflows.

(c) Sunk Cost

A sunk cost is cash already spent in the past that cannot be reversed. It has no impact on the current decision and must be excluded from capital budgeting analysis. For example, a ₹1,00,000 consultancy fee already paid to prepare a project report is irrelevant to whether the project should now be undertaken — it will be paid regardless of the decision.

(d) Working Capital

Every substantial project needs working capital. Initial working capital requirement is treated as a cash outflow; its release at the end of the project is treated as a cash inflow. No depreciation is charged on working capital, though its value might reduce by the time it's released. Additional working capital required during the project's life is a cash outflow at that time; any reduction is a cash inflow. If nothing is specified about release, it is assumed the full amount is realised at the end of the project.

(e) Allocated Overheads

Overheads allocated on a rational basis (machine hours, labour hours, material consumption, etc.) reflect expenditures already incurred and should not be treated as incremental cash flows of a new proposal. However, if overhead cost is expected to increase because of the new proposal, that incremental overhead cost is a cash outflow.

(f) Additional Capital Investment

Capital investment need not occur only at the start of a project — it can be required during the project's continuance as well. Whenever it occurs, it must be treated as a cash outflow in that period.

Formulas Used

Initial Outflow (New) = Cost of New Assets + Installation Costs + Investment in Working Capital Initial Outflow (Replace) = Cost of New Assets + Installation Costs ± Change in Net Working Capital − Net Proceeds from Sale of Old Asset ± Tax Expense/Saving on Sale Interim CF (New) = PAT + Non-Cash Expenses (Depreciation) ± Net Decrease/Increase in Working Capital Interim CF (Replace) = [Net Change in Operating Revenue/Expenses ± Net Change in Taxes] + [Net Change in Depreciation × Tax Rate] (only the depreciation TAX SHIELD is added — the full depreciation change is non-cash and already affects cash flow only through the tax figure above; adding it in full double-counts it) Terminal-Year Incremental CF = Interim Cash Flow of that year + Final Salvage Value ± Tax Saving/Expense on Disposal + Release of Net Working Capital

Why Only the Depreciation Tax Shield Counts — Full Derivation

Depreciation is a non-cash expense, so it cannot enter a cash-flow calculation twice. Below is the algebra showing why the two paths — "flow it through EBT then add it back in full" and "add only its tax shield" — collapse to the same answer, and why the tool's earlier version (adding the full rupee change) overstated cash flow.

Start from the definition of cash flow after tax (CFAT): CFAT = EBT × (1 − t) + Depreciation Incremental (Δ) form, where ΔEBT = ΔRevenue − ΔExpenses − ΔDepreciation: ΔCFAT = (ΔRev − ΔExp − ΔDep)(1 − t) + ΔDep Expand the bracket: ΔCFAT = (ΔRev − ΔExp)(1 − t) − ΔDep(1 − t) + ΔDep = (ΔRev − ΔExp)(1 − t) + ΔDep × [1 − (1 − t)] = (ΔRev − ΔExp)(1 − t) + ΔDep × t Result: the "− ΔDep(1−t)" and "+ ΔDep" terms do NOT cancel completely — they collapse to a single small term, ΔDep × t. That term is the depreciation TAX SHIELD. It is the only place depreciation belongs in the cash-flow figure.
If you instead add the FULL ΔDep on top of a tax figure that was computed on (ΔRev − ΔExp) alone, you get: Wrong CFAT = (ΔRev − ΔExp)(1 − t) + ΔDep Compare to the correct result: Correct CFAT = (ΔRev − ΔExp)(1 − t) + ΔDep × t Overstatement = Wrong − Correct = ΔDep − ΔDep×t = ΔDep × (1 − t) So for every rupee of depreciation change, adding the full amount instead of just the tax shield overstates the interim cash flow by ΔDep × (1 − t) — i.e. 70% of the depreciation figure at a 30% tax rate. This is exactly the error the earlier version of this tool made.

Block of Assets and Depreciation

Tax shield from depreciation is considered while calculating project cash flows, and taxable income follows the provisions of the applicable Income Tax Act. Depreciation treatment is based on the concept of a Block of Assets — a group of assets of the same class (building, machinery, furniture, etc.) depreciated at the same rate. Tax treatment on disposal differs depending on whether the block contains only one asset or more than one asset.

Inputs

Dashboard

WDV at the beginning of disposal year—
Depreciation charged in disposal year—
Short-term capital gain / (loss)—
Tax benefit / (tax cost)—

Formula & Rule

WDV each year = WDV(previous year) − Depreciation@rate on that WDV Case 1 — Only asset in the block (block ceases to exist): No depreciation is charged in the year of sale. Short-Term Capital Loss/(Gain) = WDV at start of year − Sale Value Tax Benefit/(Cost) = STCL/(STCG) × Tax Rate Case 2 — Other assets remain in the block: Depreciation IS charged in the year of sale, on (WDV at start of year − Sale Value), provided that figure is positive. If Sale Value > WDV at start of year, no depreciation is charged and the excess is a Short-Term Capital Gain instead. Tax Benefit on Depreciation = Depreciation × Tax Rate

This distinction matters because under the Block of Assets concept, an individual asset does not have its own depreciation schedule once pooled with others — only the block as a whole does, and gains/losses on disposal are absorbed differently depending on whether other assets remain in that block.

Exclusion of Financing Costs Principle

Why Financing Costs Are Excluded

When defining cash flows relating to long-term funds, financing costs (interest on long-term debt and equity dividend) must be excluded — they're already reflected in the Weighted Average Cost of Capital used as the discount rate. Deducting them again in the cash flows would double-count the cost of long-term funds. In practice: interest on long-term debt is ignored in computing profits and taxes, and expected dividends are irrelevant to cash flow analysis (dividends come only from post-tax profit, so they pose no difficulty; interest does, since it's usually deducted before arriving at profit after tax).

Profit After Tax excluding financing cost = Profit Before Interest & Tax × (1 − Tax Rate) = Profit After Tax + Interest × (1 − Tax Rate)

Financing-Cost Exclusion Calculator

PAT (after interest, as reported)—
Tax-adjusted interest add-back—
PAT excluding financing cost—

Post-Tax Principle

Why Cash Flows Must Be Post-Tax

Tax payments, like all other payments, must be properly deducted in deriving cash flows — cash flows must be defined in post-tax terms. It's best to avoid pre-tax cash flows discounted at a pre-tax rate; both the discount rate and the cash flows must be post-tax.

Sales Value Less: Variable Cost = Contribution Less: Fixed Cash Cost (excl. interest) and Depreciation = Earnings Before Tax (EBT) Less: Tax = Earnings After Tax (EAT) Add: Depreciation = Cash Inflow After Tax (CFAT)

Capital Budgeting Techniques — Overview

To maximise shareholder wealth, the best or most profitable investment projects must be selected — the results of a bad long-term investment decision can be devastating in both financial and strategic terms. Several appraisal techniques exist, classified as follows:

Traditional / Non-Discounting Techniques (don't discount future cash flows)
  • Payback Period
  • Accounting Rate of Return (ARR)
Time-Adjusted / Discounted Cash Flow Techniques (consider time value of money)
  • Net Present Value (NPV)
  • Profitability Index (PI)
  • Internal Rate of Return (IRR)
  • Discounted Payback Period
  • Modified Internal Rate of Return (MIRR)

Organisations may use one or more of these techniques — some use different methods for different project types, while others apply multiple methods to every project. The rest of this lab covers each technique in a logical build-up, with a live calculator for each.

Payback Period

The payback period is the length of time required for the cumulative total net cash flows from an investment to equal the total initial cash outlay — the point at which the investor has recovered all the money invested.

Inputs

Payback Dashboard

Cash flow pattern detected—
Payback period—
Payback Reciprocal (avg. cash flow / investment)—
Total cash recovered over horizon—

Formula

Uniform Cash Flows: Payback Period = Total Initial Investment / Annual Cash Inflow Non-Uniform Cash Flows: Find the year cumulative inflows reach the initial investment; Fractional year = Balance Cash Outlay Remaining / Cash Inflow of That Year Payback Reciprocal = Average Annual Cash Inflow / Initial Investment (a close approximation of IRR if the project's life is at least twice the payback period, with roughly equal annual cash inflows)
Advantages
  • Easy to compute and understand — gives a quick estimate of recovery time.
  • Serves as a rough risk indicator: longer payback, riskier project (long-term forecasts are less reliable).
  • Useful where cash/liquidity is tight or obsolescence risk is high (e.g. software industry).
Limitations
  • Ignores the time value of money — treats two projects with equal payback as equal, even if their cash-flow timing differs.
  • Ignores total profitability — cash flows after payback are ignored entirely.
  • Over-emphasises short paybacks, disadvantaging long-term projects.

Accounting (Book) Rate of Return (ARR)

ARR measures the average annual net income of a project (incremental income) as a percentage of the investment. The numerator is average annual net income over the project's useful life; the denominator can be the initial investment or the average investment.

Inputs

ARR Dashboard — All Three Versions

Average annual profit—
Version 1 — ARR on Initial Investment—
Version 2 — ARR on Total Investment (same as V1)—
Version 3 — ARR on Average Investment—

Formula

ARR = Average Annual Net Income / Investment Version 1 (Annual basis) — ARR each year = Profit that year / Investment value at start of that year, then averaged Version 2 (Total Investment basis) — ARR = Average Annual Profit / Initial Investment Version 3 (Average Investment basis) — ARR = Average Annual Profit / Average Investment where Average Investment = ½ × (Initial Investment − Salvage Value) + Salvage Value + Additional Working Capital
Advantages
  • Uses readily available accounting data — no special procedures needed.
  • May mirror the method used to evaluate operating performance, ensuring consistency between decision-making and performance evaluation.
  • Considers all net income over the entire project life.
Limitations
  • Ignores the time value of money, treating all cash flows as equal regardless of timing.
  • Depends on accounting choices (e.g. depreciation method), which can distort net income and book values.
  • Uses net income, not cash flow, as the measure — cash flow is generally the better performance measure.
  • Ignores working capital and other outlays not reflected in the asset's book value.

Net Present Value (NPV)

NPV is a discounted cash flow method that considers the time value of money: cash flow in early years is worth more than an equal amount in a later year. It uses a specified discount rate to bring all subsequent cash inflows back to their present value at the time of the initial investment (year 0).

NPV = Present Value of Cash Inflows − Present Value of Cash Outflows NPV = Σ (t=1 to n) Ct / (1+k)^t − I where C = cash flow, k = discount rate, I = investment

Inputs

NPV Dashboard

Total present value of inflows—
Net Present Value—
Decision—
Project life (years)—

Steps & Decision Rule

1. Determine net cash inflow each year→2. Select the discount rate (WACC)→3. Find each year's discount factor→4. Multiply cash flows by discount factors→5. Total all present values
NPV ≥ 0 → Accept the Proposal NPV < 0 → Reject the Proposal For mutually exclusive projects: select the project with the higher NPV.
Advantages
  • Accounts for the time value of money.
  • Considers the whole stream of cash flows.
  • Can be seen directly as the addition to shareholder wealth — in line with the basic financial objective.
  • Expressed in current rupees, so different projects' NPVs can be meaningfully compared.
Limitations
  • Involves difficult calculations.
  • Accuracy depends on accurate forecasting of cash flows and the discount rate — both can be hard to estimate in practice.
  • Being an absolute measure, it ignores differences in initial outflow/scale when evaluating mutually exclusive projects.

Profitability Index / Desirability Factor / Present Value Index (PI)

When comparing several proposals, each involving different amounts of cash inflows, the Profitability Index gives a relative measure of profitability — dividing the present value of inflows by the outflow, rather than looking at the absolute NPV.

Profitability Index (PI) = Sum of Discounted Cash Inflows / (Initial Cash Outlay or Total Discounted Cash Outflow)

Inputs

PI Dashboard

Profitability Index—
Implied NPV (Inflow − Outflow)—
Decision—
Excess return per rupee invested—

Decision Rule

PI ≥ 1 → Accept the Proposal PI < 1 → Reject the Proposal For mutually exclusive projects with the same NPV: select the project with the higher PI.

Since PI is an extension of NPV, it shares the same underlying advantages and limitations, but expresses the result per rupee invested rather than as an absolute figure — useful when comparing proposals of very different scale, such as a project needing ₹5,50,000 versus one needing ₹1,00,20,000: the larger project can have the highest absolute inflow yet the lowest desirability factor if its outflow is disproportionately larger.

Advantages
  • Also uses the time value of money.
  • Being a ratio, it's a relative measure of a project's profitability — useful for ranking.
Limitations
  • Fails as a guide under capital rationing where projects are indivisible.
  • Choosing one large high-NPV project can exclude several smaller projects that together have a higher combined NPV.
  • A lower-PI project might free up cash for another profitable project a year or two later, producing more total NPV than picking the highest-PI project alone — so PI should never be used indiscriminately without checking alternative combinations.

Internal Rate of Return (IRR)

IRR considers the time value of money, the initial investment, and all cash flows — but unlike NPV, it does not use a desired rate of return; instead it solves for the discount rate that makes the present value of subsequent cash inflows exactly equal to the initial cash outflow. That rate is then compared to a criterion/cut-off rate (typically the organisation's WACC).

Inputs

IRR Dashboard

IRR (solved by iteration)—
Sign changes in cash-flow stream—
Multiple-IRR risk—
NPV at solved IRR (should ≈ 0)—

Calculation Method & Interpolation Formula

Approximate ("fake") payback = Total Initial Investment / Annual Cash Inflow (if roughly uniform) Locate this factor in the PVAF table for the project's life to bracket two discount rates (LR, HR). Interpolation Formula: IRR = LR + [ NPV at LR / (NPV at LR − NPV at HR) ] × (HR − LR) For non-uniform cash flows: discount at a trial rate; if NPV is positive, try a higher rate (and vice versa) until NPV brackets zero between two rates, then interpolate exactly as above.

Acceptance Rule

IRR ≥ Cut-off Rate (WACC) → Accept the Proposal IRR < Cut-off Rate (WACC) → Reject the Proposal

Multiple Internal Rate of Return

When project cash flows change sign more than once during the project's life (e.g. an outflow, then inflows, then a major outflow again — common in projects with heavy decommissioning costs), there can be more than one IRR. If the cost of capital lies below both IRRs a decision is straightforward; otherwise the IRR rule can be misleading, since the project should only be accepted if the cost of capital lies between IRR₁ and IRR₂. This calculator flags the number of sign changes above as an early warning.

IRR and Mutually Exclusive Projects

IRR is a relative (percentage) measure and ignores the scale of investment. A smaller project can have a much higher IRR than a larger one, yet the larger project can add more absolute wealth (higher NPV) — accepting the smaller, higher-IRR project can mean forgoing the extra NPV the larger project would have delivered. It is not safe to assume IRR alone can rank mutually exclusive projects, even when the larger project also happens to have the higher IRR — a change in the discount rate can flip which project has the higher NPV (see the NPV vs IRR Conflicts tab).

The Reinvestment Assumption

NPV assumes all interim cash flows are reinvested at the discount rate used for NPV — a logical assumption, since NPV only accepts projects earning more than that rate. IRR, in contrast, assumes all interim cash flows are reinvested at the project's own IRR — an assumption that favours projects with cash flows concentrated in the early years, and can be unrealistic when the IRR is very high, since the firm may have no comparably attractive reinvestment opportunity actually available.

Advantages
  • Uses the time value of money.
  • Considers all cash flows in the project.
  • Easy, intuitive comparison against the cost of capital.
  • Supports the objective of maximising shareholder wealth.
Limitations
  • Tedious to calculate with multiple sign changes; multiple IRRs are hard to interpret.
  • Creates ranking problems for mutually exclusive projects with different cash-flow patterns.
  • Assumes reinvestment at the IRR itself, ignoring the firm's real ability to reinvest at a portfolio of different rates.
  • For mutually exclusive projects with very different outlay sizes, a lower-IRR project with a larger commitment can still add more absolute shareholder wealth.

Discounted Payback Period Method

Identical in spirit to the simple payback period, except the cash flows are first discounted at a predetermined rate before accumulating them — correcting the plain payback method's biggest flaw: ignoring the time value of money. This makes it a more conservative (and typically longer) payback estimate than the simple method, and the distortion between the two grows as the required rate of return increases.

Inputs

Discounted Payback Dashboard

Simple payback period (undiscounted)—
Discounted payback period—
Distortion (discounted − simple)—
Recovered by end of horizon?—

Modified Internal Rate of Return (MIRR)

MIRR addresses several IRR limitations: it eliminates the multiple-IRR problem, resolves the unrealistic reinvestment assumption, and produces results consistent with NPV. It's also called the Terminal Value method. All cash flows except the initial investment are brought forward to their terminal value using an appropriate reinvestment rate (usually the cost of capital), giving a single terminal cash inflow. MIRR is the discount rate that equates the present value of that terminal inflow to the year-0 outflow. The decision criterion is the same as IRR: accept if MIRR exceeds the required rate of return.

Inputs

MIRR Dashboard

Terminal value of all inflows—
Total return multiple (TV / Investment)—
MIRR—
Plain IRR for comparison—

Formula

Terminal Value (TV) = Σ [ Cash Flow(t) × (1 + reinvestment rate)^(n − t) ] for each year t = 1 to n MIRR = (TV / Initial Investment)^(1/n) − 1

Comparing NPV & IRR, and When They Disagree

Similarities: both are discounted cash flow methods that consider the time value of money, and both consider all cash flows over the investment's expected useful life. But for mutually exclusive projects, three scenarios can make the two methods reach different conclusions: scale/size disparity, time disparity in cash flows, and disparity in project life (unequal lives) — all ultimately rooted in the two methods' different reinvestment assumptions.

Project A

Project B

Discount Rate

Side-by-Side Comparison

■ Blue = Project A's NPV profile■ Green = Project B's NPV profile — where the lines cross is the crossover discount rate; where one line is above the axis and the other below, NPV and IRR can disagree on which project to prefer.

The Three Conflict Scenarios

Scenario 1 — Scale/Size Disparity

IRR is a relative measure, NPV an absolute one — when projects differ greatly in scale, they can rank oppositely: the smaller project often wins on IRR%, the larger on absolute NPV ₹.

Scenario 2 — Time Disparity

Even with similar total and similar-scale cash flows, if one project's inflows arrive earlier and the other's later, the reinvestment-rate assumption embedded in each method can flip the ranking.

Scenario 3 — Unequal Lives

Comparing a short-lived, front-loaded project against a longer one can rank differently under NPV versus IRR — resolved using the special-case methods in the Unequal Lives tab (Replacement Chain / Equivalent Annualised Criterion).

The default numbers pre-loaded above reproduce a classic scale-disparity example (Scenario 1): at 10% cost of capital, Project B's NPV is far higher, yet Project A's IRR is higher — a direct conflict. Net Present Value (NPV)NPV > 0 → Accept; NPV < 0 → RejectProject with the highest positive NPV
Profitability Index (PI)PI > 1 → Accept; PI < 1 → RejectWhen NPV is the same, project with the highest PI
Internal Rate of Return (IRR)IRR > cut-off (K) → Accept; IRR < K → RejectProject with the maximum IRR (with the caveats discussed in the IRR tab)

Even though IRR and PI have simple mutually-exclusive rules stated here, the worked examples throughout this lab show that NPV is the criterion that consistently gives results in conformity with the wealth-maximisation principle whenever the techniques genuinely conflict.

Capital Budgeting Under Capital Rationing

If a project has a positive NPV, it should normally be accepted to maximise shareholder wealth. But when resource (capital) constraints force a firm to choose among several positive-NPV projects, two scenarios matter: if projects are independent and divisible, rank them by NPV per rupee of capital invested; if projects are indivisible, evaluate combinations by absolute NPV within the budget.

Inputs

Capital Rationing Dashboard

Best NPV — divisible projects—
Capital used — divisible—
Best NPV — indivisible combination—
Best indivisible combination—

Bars show NPV per ₹1 invested for each project, ranked highest to lowest — the basis for the divisible allocation above.

Method

Divisible projects: Rank by NPV per ₹1 invested = NPV / Investment, then take projects in ranked order until the budget is exhausted (partial/fractional project allowed for the last one). Indivisible projects: Evaluate every combination of whole projects that fits within the budget; select the combination with the highest total absolute NPV (this calculator brute-forces every combination up to 12 projects).

Projects With Unequal Lives

Comparing mutually exclusive projects (e.g. retaining an old asset vs. replacing it, or choosing between two proposals) poses no special problem when they share the same life — but conflicts arise when project lives differ. Two methods handle this: the Replacement Chain (Common Life) Method, which extends the shorter project through repeated reinvestment until both reach a common time horizon, and the simpler Equivalent Annualised Criterion, which restates each project's NPV as an equivalent uniform annual amount.

Inputs

Equivalent Annualised Criterion Dashboard

PVAF, Project A's life—
PVAF, Project B's life—
Equivalent Annualised Value — A—
Equivalent Annualised Value — B—

Method

Step (a): Compute NPV of each project using the WACC / discounting rate. Step (b): Compute the Present Value Annuity Factor (PVAF) at that rate for each project's own life. PVAF(r, n) = [ 1 − (1+r)^−n ] / r Step (c): Equivalent Annualised Value = NPV ÷ PVAF(that project's life) Compare the two Equivalent Annualised Values directly — the higher one wins, regardless of the difference in project lives. Replacement Chain Method (conceptual alternative): extend the shorter project through a second identical reinvestment cycle until both projects reach a common multiple of their lives, then compare NPVs over that common horizon directly. The Equivalent Annualised Criterion avoids having to model that extended chain explicitly.

Adjusted Present Value (APV) — Advanced Special Case

When a project's financing decision itself changes value — for example, an all-equity firm raising perpetual debt specifically to fund a project and capture the tax benefit of debt — the value of that financing side-effect can be evaluated separately from the project's own base-case value. APV splits the two apart rather than blending them into a single adjusted discount rate.

Adjusted Present Value (APV) = Base-Case NPV (all-equity) − Issue Costs + PV of Tax Relief on Debt Interest

Inputs

APV Dashboard

Base-case NPV (all-equity)—
Total debt raised (capex + issue costs)—
PV of tax relief on debt interest (perpetuity)—
Adjusted Present Value (APV)—

Method

Base-Case NPV = − Capex + (Annual Cash Flow / Ungeared Discount Rate) Amount Raised = Capex + Issue Costs Annual Tax Relief on Interest = Amount Raised × Debt Rate × Tax Rate (in perpetuity) PV of Tax Relief = Annual Tax Relief / Debt Rate APV = Base-Case NPV − Issue Costs + PV of Tax Relief Adjusted Discount Rate (ADR): the single rate that, applied to the same annual cash flow as a perpetuity on the amount raised, would produce the same APV — solved by working backward from APV to an equivalent annual income, then expressing that income as a percentage of the amount raised. This ADR can only be reused for a future project if that project has identical business risk and is financed on identical terms — otherwise it must be recalculated from scratch.

Risk-Adjusted Discount Rate (RADR)

Every technique so far has discounted cash flows at a single rate, implicitly treating every project as equally risky. In reality, riskier projects should be discounted more heavily. The Risk-Adjusted Discount Rate method builds a risk premium directly into the discount rate itself — riskier projects get a higher rate, and therefore a lower present value for the same forecast cash flows.

Inputs

Dashboard

Risk-adjusted discount rate—
NPV at risk-adjusted rate—
NPV at risk-free rate (for comparison)—
Decision—

Formula

Risk-Adjusted Discount Rate (RADR) = Risk-Free Rate + Risk Premium (reflecting the project's risk class) NPV = Σ CFt / (1 + RADR)^t − Initial Investment

The higher the perceived risk, the larger the premium added — a routine expansion project might carry only a small premium over the risk-free rate, while an entirely new, unproven business line might carry a much larger one. The main weakness: the premium is inherently a judgment call, and a single blended rate can't distinguish between risk that changes over a project's life.

Certainty Equivalent Method

Rather than inflating the discount rate, this method adjusts the cash flows themselves — converting each uncertain, risky cash flow into a smaller, "certain" equivalent that a risk-averse decision-maker would consider just as good as gambling on the risky amount. Those certainty-equivalent cash flows are then discounted at the risk-free rate, since all the risk adjustment has already been made to the cash flows.

Inputs

Dashboard

Total certainty-equivalent cash flow—
NPV using certainty equivalents—
Decision—

Formula

Certainty-Equivalent Cash Flow (Year t) = Expected Cash Flow(t) × Coefficient αt (0 ≤ αt ≤ 1) NPV = Σ [CFt × αt] / (1 + Risk-Free Rate)^t − Initial Investment

Coefficients typically decline over time, since cash flows further in the future are harder to forecast reliably. Unlike RADR, this method can apply a different degree of risk adjustment to each individual year's cash flow — a genuine advantage when a project's risk profile changes over its life (e.g. high uncertainty early, more predictable later).

Probability Assignment & Expected NPV

Instead of a single forecast, this approach assigns probabilities to several possible outcomes — pessimistic, most likely, optimistic — and computes a probability-weighted expected NPV, which is a far more informative single number than any one scenario alone.

Inputs

Dashboard

Expected NPV—
Best-case NPV—
Worst-case NPV—
Probability sum (should = 1.00)—

Formula

NPV(scenario i) = Σ CFt(i) / (1+r)^t − Initial Investment Expected NPV = Σ [ Probability(i) × NPV(scenario i) ]

Standard Deviation & Coefficient of Variation of NPV

Expected NPV alone doesn't say how risky a project is — two projects can share the same expected NPV while one is far more volatile. Standard deviation measures that spread in absolute rupee terms; the coefficient of variation (standard deviation ÷ expected NPV) makes risk comparable between projects of different sizes.

Inputs

Dashboard

Expected NPV—
Standard deviation of NPV—
Coefficient of variation—
Risk interpretation—

Formula

Expected NPV, E(NPV) = Σ [ Probability(i) × NPV(i) ] Variance = Σ [ Probability(i) × (NPV(i) − E(NPV))² ] Standard Deviation, σ = √Variance Coefficient of Variation, CV = σ / E(NPV)

When comparing two mutually exclusive projects, the one with the lower coefficient of variation carries less risk per rupee of expected return — a more decision-useful comparison than standard deviation alone whenever the projects differ in scale.

Decision Tree Analysis

Many real investment decisions unfold in stages — an initial, smaller commitment (e.g. a pilot or test-market), followed by a much larger follow-on investment only if the first stage succeeds. A decision tree maps out these sequential decisions and chance events, and is solved by rolling back from the final branches to the first decision, at each chance node taking the probability-weighted average of what follows.

Stage 1 — Initial (Test) Investment

Stage 2 — Follow-On Investment (only if Stage 1 succeeds)

Roll-Back Dashboard

Stage 2 expected value if pursued—
Stage 2 NPV (invest, if given the choice)—
Expected value at Stage 1 (rolled back)—
Overall decision-tree NPV—

Method — Rolling Back the Tree

Step 1: At the final (Stage 2) decision node, compute the expected PV of continuing: EV(Stage 2 outcomes) = P(high)×PV(high) + P(low)×PV(low) Step 2: Compare EV(Stage 2 outcomes) − Stage 2 Investment against the alternative (usually 0/abandon); take the better of the two — this is the value of reaching the "success" branch. Step 3: Roll back to Stage 1: Expected Value = P(success)×[value of success branch] + P(failure)×[value of failure branch] Step 4: Overall NPV = Expected Value at Stage 1 − Stage 1 Investment

Scenario Analysis

A simpler, non-probability-weighted cousin of the probability approach: build out a small number of complete, internally consistent scenarios — typically best case, most likely case, and worst case — each with its own full set of assumptions, and see the resulting range of NPVs. Useful for quickly communicating a project's risk to people who find probability distributions harder to interpret.

Inputs

Dashboard

Worst-case NPV—
Most-likely-case NPV—
Best-case NPV—
NPV swing (best − worst)—

Simulation Approach (Monte Carlo)

Where scenario analysis picks only two or three fixed cases, simulation runs the project through hundreds or thousands of randomly generated outcomes, each year's cash flow drawn from a probability distribution, to build up a full distribution of possible NPVs — not just a range, but a sense of how likely each outcome is, including the probability of a loss. This lab runs a genuine live simulation with the trial count you choose.

Inputs

Simulation Results

Mean simulated NPV—
Std. deviation of simulated NPV—
Probability NPV < 0—
Trials run—

Histogram of simulated NPV outcomes across all trials — each bar is one NPV range (bucket), height shows how many trials landed there.

Method

For each of N trials: For each year t = 1..n: draw a random cash flow from a Normal(mean, std. dev.) distribution Compute that trial's NPV by discounting the drawn cash flows at the given rate After all trials: report the mean NPV, standard deviation of NPV, and the proportion of trials with NPV < 0 (Random normal draws generated here using the Box–Muller transform.)

Replacement Analysis

A common real-world capital budgeting decision: should an old asset be replaced with a new one? The right approach is incremental — compare the new asset's costs and benefits only against what the old asset would otherwise have delivered, not in isolation.

Old Asset

New Asset

Incremental Analysis Dashboard

Tax effect on sale of old asset—
Incremental initial outflow—
Incremental annual cash flow—
Incremental NPV—
Incremental IRR—
Decision—

Formula

Tax Effect on Sale of Old Asset = (Book Value − Sale Value) × Tax Rate [positive = tax saving, if sold below book value] Incremental Initial Outflow = Cost of New Asset − Sale Value of Old Asset − Tax Effect on Sale Incremental Annual Cash Flow = Cash Flow with New Asset − Cash Flow if Old Asset Were Kept Incremental Terminal Cash Flow = Incremental Annual CF (final year) + Salvage Value of New Asset Incremental NPV = PV of Incremental Cash Flows − Incremental Initial Outflow

Inflation-Adjusted Capital Budgeting

Cash flows and discount rates can each be expressed in nominal (money-of-the-day, including inflation) or real (constant purchasing power, inflation stripped out) terms. The critical rule — a frequent exam trap — is consistency: nominal cash flows must be discounted at the nominal rate, and real cash flows at the real rate. Mixing the two produces a wrong answer, in either direction.

Inputs

Dashboard — Both Methods Should Agree

Nominal discount rate (Fisher equation)—
NPV — Method 1: Real CF at Real Rate—
NPV — Method 2: Nominal CF at Nominal Rate—
Difference (should ≈ 0)—

Formula — The Fisher Equation

(1 + Nominal Rate) = (1 + Real Rate) × (1 + Inflation Rate) Method 1 (Real): NPV = Σ Real CFt / (1 + Real Rate)^t − Investment Method 2 (Nominal): Nominal CFt = Real CFt × (1 + Inflation Rate)^t NPV = Σ Nominal CFt / (1 + Nominal Rate)^t − Investment

Both methods must give the same NPV when applied consistently — this calculator runs both side by side specifically to demonstrate that, and to make the mismatch obvious if real cash flows are ever accidentally discounted at a nominal rate (or vice versa).

Two-way sensitivity

Interactive NPV Heatmap: Discount Rate × Cash-Flow Change

This visualisation helps students see how NPV changes when two assumptions move together: required return and operating cash-flow forecast. Green cells indicate positive NPV; red cells indicate negative NPV.

Inputs

Heatmap

How to Interpret

If many cells around the base case are green, the project is robust. If small changes turn cells red, the project is sensitive and needs risk controls. If nearly all cells are red, the project is weak unless strategic benefits justify it.

Modern decision support

AI Use in Capital Budgeting Decision Making

AI does not replace NPV, WACC, cash-flow estimation or managerial judgement. It improves capital budgeting by helping forecast inputs, detect risk, run scenarios, find inconsistencies, summarise assumptions and support post-audit learning.

Where AI Helps

  • Forecasting: demand, price, cost, inflation, maintenance, downtime.
  • Risk detection: unusual assumptions, optimism bias, missing variables.
  • Scenario generation: best/base/worst and stress cases.
  • Document review: extracting assumptions from proposals and contracts.
  • Portfolio selection: ranking projects under capital constraints.
  • Post-audit: comparing actual vs forecast and identifying learning patterns.

Where AI Must Be Controlled

  • AI can hallucinate facts, rates, tax rules and formulas.
  • AI output must be checked by finance professionals.
  • Confidential project data must be protected.
  • Model assumptions should be explainable and auditable.
  • AI should not override legal, ESG or board-level constraints.

India-focused application

Indian-Based Capital Budgeting Case Studies

These cases use Indian business conditions such as GST effects, Make in India manufacturing, renewable energy, infrastructure, rupee inflation, working-capital cycles and regulatory constraints.

Case India 1: Solar Rooftop for a Factory

A Delhi/NCR manufacturing unit evaluates rooftop solar to reduce electricity cost. Initial cost includes panels, inverter, installation and safety approvals. Benefits include lower electricity bills, accelerated depreciation, possible subsidy and ESG value.

Tasks:
  1. Estimate after-tax annual savings.
  2. Include depreciation tax shield.
  3. Test sensitivity to electricity tariff escalation.
  4. Discuss ESG and carbon benefit.

Case India 2: EV Delivery Fleet

An e-commerce distributor compares electric two-wheelers with petrol vehicles. EVs have higher upfront cost but lower running cost and maintenance. Battery replacement and charging infrastructure are important.

Tasks:
  1. Prepare incremental cash flows.
  2. Include battery replacement as future outflow.
  3. Compute NPV and payback.
  4. Discuss fuel-price risk and government incentives.

Case India 3: MSME CNC Machine Replacement

An MSME considers replacing an old machine with a CNC machine. Benefits include labour savings, lower rejection rate and higher capacity. Risks include operator training, downtime and financing constraints.

Tasks:
  1. Calculate replacement initial outlay after sale of old machine.
  2. Include training and working capital.
  3. Analyse NPV, IRR and discounted payback.
  4. Discuss capital rationing for MSMEs.

Case India 4: Cold Storage Project

An agribusiness evaluates a cold storage facility. Cash flows depend on utilisation, electricity cost, maintenance, spoilage reduction and government support.

Tasks:
  1. Build best/base/worst utilisation scenarios.
  2. Include working capital and maintenance.
  3. Calculate expected NPV.
  4. Discuss social benefits to farmers.

Indian Context Checklist

Tax & policy

Depreciation rates, GST input credits, incentives, subsidies and tax holidays.

Macroeconomic factors

Inflation, interest rates, rupee movement, fuel and power prices.

Operational realities

Working-capital cycle, supplier reliability, logistics, permits and compliance.

Global application

International Capital Budgeting Case Studies

International projects require currency conversion, political risk, remittance rules, withholding tax, inflation differences and country-specific discount rates.

Case Global 1: Indian Company Setting Up Plant in Vietnam

Cash flows are in VND/USD but parent evaluates returns in INR. The project has local tax, remittance limits and exchange-rate uncertainty.

  1. Forecast foreign currency cash flows.
  2. Convert to INR using expected exchange rates.
  3. Deduct withholding tax on remittances.
  4. Use home-currency discount rate and compute NPV.

Case Global 2: US Software Firm Opening India Development Centre

The firm invests in office, hiring and training in India. Benefits are lower development cost and 24-hour delivery capability.

  1. Identify cost savings versus offshore setup costs.
  2. Include wage inflation and exchange risk.
  3. Analyse real options to expand team size.
  4. Discuss data security and compliance risk.

Case Global 3: Mining Project in Africa

Large initial outlay, long life, rehabilitation cost, commodity-price volatility and political risk.

  1. Use scenario analysis for commodity prices.
  2. Include closure/restoration cost in terminal cash flow.
  3. Consider APV if project debt has special terms.
  4. Discuss ESG and community impact.

Case Global 4: European Green Hydrogen Project

Benefits depend on carbon prices, subsidies, technology learning and energy cost.

  1. Estimate subsidy-adjusted initial outlay.
  2. Include carbon-credit benefits.
  3. Use real options for staged expansion.
  4. Run sensitivity on energy price and carbon price.

Global Project Risk Matrix

RiskCapital Budgeting Treatment
Exchange rateConvert cash flows consistently or use foreign discount rate.
Inflation differentialUse PPP/nominal consistency.
Political riskAdd risk premium, scenario analysis or insurance cost.
Blocked fundsDiscount expected delayed remittances separately.
Withholding taxDeduct from remitted cash flows.
Country ESG rulesInclude compliance costs and strategic constraints.

Complete Concept Notes

These notes summarise the full conceptual base of capital budgeting in exam-friendly language.

Capital Budgeting Meaning

Capital budgeting is the process of making long-term investment decisions involving acquisition, replacement, expansion, modernisation or disposal of fixed assets and strategic projects. It compares expected future benefits with present investment outlay.

Nature

  • Long-term impact
  • Large investment
  • Risk and uncertainty
  • Irreversible or costly to reverse
  • Affects profitability, liquidity and strategy

Objectives

  • Maximise shareholder wealth
  • Allocate scarce capital efficiently
  • Support strategic growth
  • Control risk and liquidity
  • Replace inefficient assets
  • Comply with legal, safety or environmental requirements

Key Principle

Accept projects that increase present wealth after considering risk, tax, timing, opportunity costs, capital constraints and strategic effects.

Classification of Decisions

Replacement

Old asset is replaced to reduce cost or improve efficiency.

Expansion

Capacity is increased for existing products or markets.

Diversification

Firm enters new product, technology or market area.

Independent

Acceptance of one does not affect another.

Mutually Exclusive

Only one of competing alternatives can be selected.

Contingent

One project depends on acceptance of another.

Cash Flow Masterclass

Most capital budgeting errors happen before the NPV formula — in cash-flow estimation. This masterclass gives a complete rulebook.

Golden Rules

1. Use cash flows, not accounting profits. 2. Use incremental flows: include only changes caused by the project. 3. Use post-tax flows. 4. Exclude financing costs if discounting at WACC. 5. Exclude sunk costs. 6. Include opportunity costs. 7. Include working capital investment and recovery. 8. Include tax effects of depreciation and asset disposal. 9. Include cannibalisation and externalities. 10. Include terminal-year adjustments.

Initial Outlay Checklist

  • Purchase price of asset
  • Installation, freight and training
  • Site preparation
  • Initial working capital
  • Opportunity cost of existing assets used
  • Less sale proceeds of old asset
  • Plus/minus tax on sale of old asset
  • Government subsidy or grant

Annual Operating Cash Flow Checklist

  • Incremental revenue
  • Cost savings
  • Variable and fixed cash costs
  • Cannibalisation of existing contribution
  • Incremental overheads
  • Tax on operating profit
  • Depreciation tax shield
  • Maintenance and downtime costs

Terminal Cash Flow Checklist

  • Final year operating CFAT
  • Salvage/sale proceeds
  • Tax on gain or saving on loss
  • Working capital recovery
  • Restoration/dismantling cost
  • Environmental closure cost
  • Residual inventory disposal

Cash Flow Timeline Template

Year 0: − Initial Outlay Year 1 to n−1: Operating CFAT Year n: Operating CFAT + Terminal Cash Flow Adjustments NPV = PV(all future cash flows) − initial outlay

PaybackRecovery timeLiquidity and risk screeningIgnores post-payback cash flows and time valueShorter than maximum acceptable payback

MIRRReturn with realistic reinvestment rateAlternative to IRRRequires chosen reinvestment rateAccept if MIRR ≥ required return

Capital Budgeting Decision Playbook

Use this playbook to choose the right method for each situation.

SituationPrimary MethodSupporting AnalysisWarning
Independent projectNPVIRR, PI, paybackDo not accept negative NPV because payback is short.
Mutually exclusive, same lifeHighest NPVCrossover rate, IRR, PIIRR can prefer a smaller project.
Mutually exclusive, unequal lifeEAC/EAV or replacement chainNPV over common horizonRaw NPV can favour longer project unfairly.
Capital rationingMaximise total package NPVPI ranking if divisiblePI ranking alone can fail if indivisible.
ReplacementIncremental NPVTax on old asset sale, EACIgnore historical cost except for tax effects.
Lease vs buyLower PV costNet advantage to leasingCompare financing form, not operating benefits twice.
High uncertaintyNPV + risk analysisScenario, simulation, decision treeSingle forecast is not enough.
International projectHome-currency NPVFX, withholding tax, country riskDo not mix currencies inconsistently.
Strategic flexibilityExpanded NPVReal optionsDocument option-value assumptions.

India context

India Tax, GST and Regulatory Notes for Capital Budgeting

Study note: This is an educational checklist, not tax/legal advice. Actual treatment depends on current law, asset class, entity type and professional advice.

Income Tax Considerations

  • Depreciation rates may differ by asset block.
  • Tax shield depends on taxable profit availability.
  • Sale of asset can create balancing effects under block-of-assets rules.
  • Tax holidays, incentives and subsidies may materially change NPV.
  • MAT/AMT or loss carry-forward can affect timing of tax benefits.

GST and Indirect Tax Considerations

  • GST paid on capital goods may be available as input tax credit if eligible.
  • If ITC is available, GST should not be treated as final project cost.
  • If ITC is blocked, GST becomes part of relevant cost.
  • Output GST is generally collected from customers and not revenue.
  • Working-capital impact may arise from timing of GST payments and credits.

Regulatory and Approval Considerations

  • Environmental clearance
  • Factory licence and safety compliance
  • Pollution control approvals
  • Land-use permissions
  • Power connection and grid approvals
  • Import duties and customs clearance for imported machinery

India-Specific Risk Factors

  • Interest-rate movement
  • Rupee depreciation for imported equipment
  • Policy changes in subsidies/incentives
  • Electricity tariff escalation
  • Logistics and infrastructure bottlenecks
  • Working-capital delays due to receivables

India Project Checklist

Check: GST ITC eligibility → depreciation block/rate → subsidy taxability → import duty/customs → working capital cycle → regulatory approvals → environmental compliance → financing scheme → sensitivity for inflation and interest rates.
Print-friendly revision

Printable One-Page Capital Budgeting Summary

Use this as a final revision page before exams. You can print this tab from the browser.

Capital Budgeting in One Page

1. Identify decision type: independent, mutually exclusive, replacement, rationing, lease-buy, international, social/strategic. 2. Build timeline: Year 0, annual years, terminal year. 3. Estimate relevant post-tax incremental cash flows. 4. Exclude sunk costs and financing costs; include opportunity costs, working capital, tax shields and terminal value. 5. Select discount rate: WACC for average-risk projects; CAPM/project rate for different-risk projects. 6. Compute NPV first; use IRR, MIRR, PI, payback and ARR as supporting tools. 7. Resolve conflicts: NPV dominates for same-life mutually exclusive projects; EAC/EAV for unequal lives. 8. Analyse risk: sensitivity, scenario, expected NPV, CV, decision tree and simulation. 9. Check capital rationing, ESG, strategic fit, regulatory constraints and governance. 10. Write recommendation: accept/reject/choose option, with reason and risk notes.

Must-Remember Formulas

  • NPV = Σ CFt/(1+k)^t − I0
  • PI = PV inflows / initial outlay
  • CFAT = EBIT(1−T)+Dep
  • Tax shield = Dep × T
  • WACC = E/V Ke + D/V Kd(1−T)
  • CAPM = Rf + β(Rm−Rf)
  • EAC = PV cost / PVAF
  • MIRR = (TV/PV outflows)^(1/n)−1

Most Common Exam Traps

  • Including sunk cost
  • Ignoring opportunity cost
  • Forgetting working capital recovery
  • Deducting interest and also using WACC
  • Mixing real and nominal figures
  • Choosing IRR over NPV in conflict
  • Ignoring tax on salvage
  • Comparing unequal lives using raw NPV only

How to Use References

Read theory from textbooks, practise calculations in this HTML lab, validate formulas in Excel, and use case studies to connect numbers with managerial judgement.

Formula Derivations and Logic

Understanding derivations helps prevent formula misuse.

NPV Logic

Value today of future cash flow Ct = Ct/(1+k)^t Total present value of inflows = Σ Ct/(1+k)^t Net value added = PV inflows − initial outlay Therefore: NPV = Σ Ct/(1+k)^t − I0

Depreciation Tax Shield

Cash flow = (Revenue − Cash cost − Dep)(1−T) + Dep = (Revenue − Cash cost)(1−T) − Dep(1−T) + Dep = (Revenue − Cash cost)(1−T) + Dep×T Therefore depreciation affects cash flow only through Dep×T.

PVAF Derivation

PV of annuity = A/(1+r) + A/(1+r)^2 + ... + A/(1+r)^n This is a finite geometric series. PVAF = [1 − (1+r)^−n]/r PV = A × PVAF

MIRR Logic

Step 1: Compound all positive cash flows to terminal value at reinvestment rate. Step 2: Discount all negative cash flows to present value at finance rate. Step 3: MIRR = (TV positive cash flows / PV negative cash flows)^(1/n) − 1

IRR Interpolation

When NPV is positive at lower rate LR and negative at higher rate HR: IRR ≈ LR + [NPV_LR / (NPV_LR − NPV_HR)] × (HR − LR) This is a straight-line approximation between two NPV points.

Step-by-Step Solution Templates

Template 1: Standard NPV Problem

  1. Write initial investment at year 0.
  2. List annual cash inflows/outflows.
  3. Identify discount rate.
  4. Compute discount factors.
  5. Multiply each cash flow by factor.
  6. Sum present values.
  7. Subtract initial outlay.
  8. State accept/reject decision.

Template 2: Replacement Problem

  1. Find cost of new asset plus installation.
  2. Deduct after-tax sale proceeds of old asset.
  3. Add incremental working capital.
  4. Compute incremental annual cash flows.
  5. Add terminal salvage and WC recovery.
  6. Discount incremental flows.
  7. Accept replacement if incremental NPV is positive.

Template 3: Capital Rationing

  1. List investment and NPV for each project.
  2. If divisible, rank by PI or NPV per rupee.
  3. If indivisible, test feasible combinations.
  4. Select package with highest total NPV within budget.
  5. State unused capital, if any.

Template 4: Unequal-Life Projects

  1. Compute NPV of each project.
  2. Compute PVAF for each life.
  3. Divide NPV or PV cost by PVAF.
  4. For benefits: choose higher EAV.
  5. For costs: choose lower EAC.

Presentation Format for Answers

Given → Working → Formula → Substitution → Result → Decision → Reason Always write the decision in words, not just the number.
Fast revision

Quick Revision Cheat Sheets

Use these one-page style summaries before class tests, exams, viva and assignments.

Core Decision Rules

NPV ≥ 0 → Accept independent project NPV < 0 → Reject independent project Mutually exclusive same-life projects → choose highest NPV Unequal-life alternatives → use EAC/EAV or replacement chain Capital rationing → maximise total NPV of feasible package Lease vs buy → choose lower present value cost Replacement → accept if incremental NPV is positive

Cash-Flow Inclusion Rule

Include: incremental revenue, cost savings, opportunity cost, working capital, tax shields, after-tax salvage, cannibalisation, incremental overheads. Exclude: sunk cost, allocated non-incremental overhead, interest, dividends, historical cost except for tax effect.

Formula Snapshot

NPV = Σ CFt/(1+k)^t − I0 PI = PV inflows / Initial outlay IRR: NPV = 0 MIRR = (Terminal value / Investment)^(1/n) − 1 WACC = E/V Ke + D/V Kd(1−T) CFAT = EBIT(1−T)+Depreciation Tax Shield = Depreciation × Tax Rate

Risk Tools Snapshot

  • Sensitivity: one variable changes.
  • Scenario: full best/base/worst cases.
  • Probability: expected NPV.
  • Standard deviation/CV: risk measurement.
  • Simulation: distribution of NPVs.
  • Decision tree: staged decisions.
  • Real options: flexibility value.

Last-Minute Exam Checklist

Before calculating

Draw timeline, identify decision type, mark cash-flow years.

While calculating

Use post-tax incremental cash flows and correct discount rate.

After calculating

State decision, reason, risk and any limitations.

Common error correction

Mistake Clinic: How Students Lose Marks

This tab explains the most common capital budgeting mistakes and how to fix them.

MistakeWhy It Is WrongCorrect Treatment
Including sunk costPast cost cannot change with the decision.Ignore sunk cost; disclose only if needed.
Ignoring opportunity costUsing an asset consumes its alternative sale/use value.Include current after-tax market value as outflow.
Deducting interest in cash flowsWACC already includes financing cost.Exclude interest and dividends from project cash flow.
Forgetting working capital recoveryWorking capital tied up is often released at project end.Add recovery as terminal inflow.
Adding full depreciation as cash inflow incorrectlyDepreciation is non-cash; only tax effect matters.Use EBIT(1−T)+Dep or add depreciation tax shield.
Using IRR to rank mutually exclusive projectsIRR can mis-rank scale/timing differences.Use NPV as primary rule.
Comparing unequal lives by raw NPV onlyLonger projects may look better just because they last longer.Use EAC/EAV or replacement chain.
Mixing nominal and real figuresInflation treatment becomes inconsistent.Nominal CF with nominal rate; real CF with real rate.
Using PI ranking for indivisible projects blindlyBest package may not follow strict PI order.Evaluate feasible combinations.
No final recommendationNumbers alone do not answer the decision question.Write accept/reject/choose project and explain why.

Self-Correction Prompt

After solving any problem, ask: Did I include only incremental post-tax cash flows? Did I use the correct discount rate? Did I handle terminal value? Did I state a clear decision?

Capital Budgeting Case Studies

Use these for classroom discussion, assignments or self-practice.

Case 1: Manufacturing Automation

A manufacturing firm is considering an automated machine to reduce labour cost and improve quality. The machine has high upfront cost, training expenses, annual maintenance and salvage value. Existing workers may be redeployed.

Questions
  1. Identify relevant cash flows.
  2. Should training be capitalised in the initial outlay?
  3. How should labour savings and maintenance be treated?
  4. Which risk factors should be tested?

Case 2: New Product Launch

A company wants to launch a new product that may cannibalise an existing product. Marketing forecasts are optimistic and require additional working capital.

Questions
  1. How should cannibalisation be included?
  2. What sensitivity variables matter most?
  3. Would PI or NPV be better under a budget limit?
  4. What real options exist?

Case 3: Solar Energy Investment

A firm can install solar panels to reduce electricity cost. The project has subsidy, carbon benefits and maintenance cost.

Questions
  1. Calculate private NPV.
  2. Add social/environmental benefits.
  3. How does subsidy affect initial outlay?
  4. What non-financial factors matter?

Case 4: International Expansion

A company plans to set up a plant abroad. Cash flows are in foreign currency and remittances face withholding tax and exchange-rate risk.

Questions
  1. Convert foreign cash flows to home currency.
  2. How should country risk be handled?
  3. What happens if funds are blocked?
  4. Should APV be considered?

Mini Projects and Assignments

Mini Project 1

Build an Excel model for a 5-year project with initial outlay, depreciation, tax, working capital and terminal value. Compute NPV, IRR, MIRR, PI, payback and discounted payback.

Mini Project 2

Compare two machines with unequal lives using EAC. Include maintenance cost, downtime and salvage values.

Mini Project 3

Prepare a capital rationing recommendation for 8 projects under a fixed budget. Compare PI ranking with brute-force combination.

Mini Project 4

Mini Project 5

Mini Project 6

Prepare a post-audit report comparing forecast versus actual cash flows for a completed project.

Viva and Theory Answer Bank

QuestionModel Answer
Why is NPV superior to payback?NPV considers time value, all project cash flows and direct wealth addition. Payback focuses only on recovery period and ignores cash flows after payback.
Why exclude interest from project cash flows?Interest is part of financing cost and is already reflected in WACC. Deducting it in cash flows and discounting at WACC double-counts financing cost.
What is the difference between IRR and MIRR?IRR assumes reinvestment at IRR and can have multiple rates; MIRR assumes reinvestment at a specified realistic rate and gives a single return.
What is capital rationing?Capital rationing occurs when funds are limited and the firm cannot accept all positive-NPV projects, so it must select the best combination.
What is opportunity cost?Opportunity cost is the benefit forgone by using a resource in the project instead of its next-best alternative. It is relevant and included.
What is sunk cost?Sunk cost is already incurred and cannot be changed by the decision. It is irrelevant and excluded.
What are real options?Real options are managerial flexibilities such as deferring, expanding, abandoning, switching or staging a project.
Why use EAC?EAC converts different-life projects into equivalent annual cost, allowing fair comparison when alternatives provide similar service for unequal periods.

Full CSV content attached as an HTML tab: 500 project cases with answers.

Project IDTypeProblemAnswer
1NPV ExpansionProject requires ₹418,500, generates annual CF ₹97,750 for 4 years, rate 9%. Compute NPV.PVAF=3.240; NPV=₹-101,817; decision=Reject / redesign.
2ReplacementReplacement case: New machine cost ₹437,000; old machine sale value ₹62,200; old book value ₹97,200; tax rate 30%; incremental annual cash flow ₹52,500; life 5 years; discount rate 10%. Decide whether to replace.Tax saving on sale = (₹97,200−₹62,200)×30% = ₹10,500. Incremental outlay = ₹364,300. PV inflows = ₹52,500×3.791=₹199,016. Incremental NPV = ₹-165,284. Decision: Do not replace.
3Lease vs BuyLease-buy case: Equipment can be bought for ₹455,500 or leased for ₹92,700 per year for 6 years. Tax rate 30%, after-tax discount rate 11%, straight-line depreciation, salvage ₹36,440. Choose lease or buy.PV lease cost = lease×(1−T)×PVAF = ₹274,520. PV buy cost = price − PV depreciation shields − PV salvage = ₹339,667. Net advantage to leasing = ₹65,148. Decision: Lease.
4Capital RationingCapital rationing case: Budget ₹308,100. Projects A, B, C, D require ₹104,280, ₹132,720, ₹161,160, ₹85,320 and have NPVs ₹47,700, ₹65,720, ₹78,440, ₹37,100. Select best package.Evaluate feasible combinations because projects are indivisible. Best package = B + C; investment ₹293,880; total NPV ₹144,160. Choose this package.
5Risk ScenarioRisk scenario case: Worst NPV ₹-93,134 probability 25%, base NPV ₹29,366 probability 50%, best NPV ₹212,616 probability 25%. Find expected NPV and decision.Expected NPV = 0.25×₹-93,134+0.50×₹29,366+0.25×₹212,616=₹44,554. Decision: Accept if risk is tolerable.
6InternationalInternational case: Initial INR investment ₹511,000; annual foreign cash flow 37,100; expected exchange rate ₹84.10/FC; withholding tax 7%; life 9; INR discount rate 14%. Compute home-currency NPV.Annual remittance = 37,100×₹84.10×(1−7%) = ₹2,901,702. NPV = ₹2,901,702×4.946−₹511,000=₹13,841,899. Decision: Accept.
7Real OptionsReal options case: Static NPV ₹-268,642; option to defer ₹32,100; option to expand ₹53,150; option to abandon ₹26,750. Find expanded NPV.Expanded NPV = static NPV + option values = ₹-156,642. Decision: Reject unless strategic reasons dominate.
8Social CBASocial CBA case: Private NPV ₹-220,613; PV of social benefits ₹98,000; PV of social costs ₹38,600. Compute social NPV.Social NPV = ₹-220,613+₹98,000−₹38,600=₹-161,213. Social decision: Reject/redesign.
9WACC/CAPMWACC/CAPM case: Rf 6%, market return 13%, project beta 0.8, pre-tax debt cost 12%, tax 30%, debt weight 30%. Estimate project WACC.Ke = 6% + 0.8×(13%−6%) = 11.60%. After-tax Kd = 8.40%. WACC = 70%×Ke + 30%×Kd(1−T) = 10.64%.
10Economic LifeEconomic life case: Asset cost ₹585,000; operating cost rises every year; salvage value falls every year; discount rate 9%. Explain how to choose replacement year.Compute PV total cost for each possible life: initial cost + PV operating costs − PV salvage. Convert each to EAC = PV cost/PVAF. Choose the year with minimum EAC.
11Inflation AdjustmentInflation case: Real annual CF ₹125,250; real discount rate 8%; inflation 9%; life 7; initial investment ₹603,500. Find nominal discount rate and real-method NPV.Nominal rate = (1+8%)(1+9%)−1 = 17.72%. Real-method NPV = ₹48,598. Use nominal cash flows only with nominal rate.
12Working CapitalWorking capital case: Initial asset investment ₹622,000; working capital ₹74,640; annual CF ₹128,000; WC recovered at end; life 8; rate 11%. Compute NPV.Year-0 outflow = asset + WC = ₹696,640. PV inflows = ₹658,704; PV WC recovery = ₹32,388. NPV = ₹-5,548. Decision: Reject.
13Depreciation Tax ShieldDepreciation shield case: Asset cost ₹640,500; life 9; straight-line depreciation; tax rate 30%; discount rate 12%. Compute annual and PV tax shield.Annual depreciation = ₹71,167. Annual tax shield = ₹21,350. PV tax shield = ₹21,350×5.328=₹113,758.
14APVAPV case: Base-case NPV ₹-343,786; debt raised ₹329,500; corporate tax 30%; issue costs ₹13,180. Estimate APV using perpetual debt tax shield.PV debt tax shield = Debt×T = ₹98,850. APV = base NPV + tax shield − issue cost = ₹-258,116. Decision: Reject.
15Decision TreeDecision tree case: Stage-1 cost ₹101,625; success probability 0.70. If successful, invest ₹440,375; high PV ₹1,016,250 probability 0.6; low PV ₹372,625. Find rollback NPV.Stage-2 NPV = 0.6×₹1,016,250+0.4×₹372,625−₹440,375=₹318,425. Overall NPV = 0.70×max(Stage-2 NPV,0)−₹101,625=₹121,273. Decision: Proceed.
16SensitivitySensitivity case: Base project has initial investment ₹696,000, annual CF ₹139,000, life 5, rate 15%. Test NPV if annual CF falls/rises by 10%.Base NPV = ₹-230,050. Downside NPV = ₹-276,645. Upside NPV = ₹-183,455. If downside becomes negative, project is cash-flow sensitive.
17Scenario AnalysisScenario case: Initial investment ₹714,500; life 6; rate 16%. Worst/base/best annual CFs are ₹106,312, ₹141,750, ₹177,188. Compute scenario NPVs.Worst NPV ₹-322,767; base NPV ₹-192,189; best NPV ₹-61,611. Interpret whether the range crosses zero.
18MIRRMIRR case: Investment ₹733,000; annual CF ₹144,500 for 7 years; reinvestment rate 8%. Compute MIRR.Terminal value of inflows = ₹1,289,345. MIRR = (TV/I)^(1/n)−1 = 8.40%. Compare with required return.
19Discounted PaybackDiscounted payback case: Investment ₹751,500; annual CF ₹147,250; rate 9%; life 8. Compute discounted payback.Cumulative discounted inflows by year 8 = ₹815,002. Discounted payback = 7.14 years.
20Profitability IndexPI case: Investment ₹770,000; annual CF ₹150,000; life 9; discount rate 10%. Compute PI.PV inflows = ₹863,854. PI = PV inflows / investment = 1.122. Decision: Accept.
21ESG ProjectESG case: Private NPV ₹-415,223; estimated PV of carbon/community benefit ₹58,400. Compute adjusted ESG NPV.Adjusted NPV = private NPV + ESG benefit = ₹-356,823. Still document assumptions and avoid double counting.
22AI InvestmentAI investment case: AI system setup cost ₹807,000; expected annual savings ₹155,500; confidence factor 85%; life 4; rate 12%. Compute confidence-adjusted NPV.Adjusted annual savings = ₹132,175. NPV = adjusted savings×PVAF − setup = ₹-405,538. Decision: Pilot first / redesign.

Tax rate 30%, after-tax discount rate 14%, straight-line depreciation, salvage ₹746,840. Choose lease or buy.PV lease cost = lease×(1−T)×PVAF = ₹852,712. PV buy cost = price − PV depreciation shields − PV salvage = ₹6,664,045. Net advantage to leasing = ₹5,811,332. Decision: Lease.
484Capital RationingCapital rationing case: Budget ₹6,080,100. Projects A, B, C, D require ₹2,057,880, ₹2,619,120, ₹3,180,360, ₹1,683,720 and have NPVs ₹641,700, ₹884,120, ₹1,055,240, ₹499,099. Select best package.Evaluate feasible combinations because projects are indivisible. Best package = B + C; investment ₹5,799,480; total NPV ₹1,939,360. Choose this package.
485Risk ScenarioRisk scenario case: Worst NPV ₹-5,056,853 probability 25%, base NPV ₹-4,694,353 probability 50%, best NPV ₹-4,199,103 probability 25%. Find expected NPV and decision.Expected NPV = 0.25×₹-5,056,853+0.50×₹-4,694,353+0.25×₹-4,199,103=₹-4,661,165. Decision: Reject or redesign.
486InternationalInternational case: Initial INR investment ₹9,391,000; annual foreign cash flow 205,100; expected exchange rate ₹84.10/FC; withholding tax 7%; life 6; INR discount rate 8%. Compute home-currency NPV.Annual remittance = 205,100×₹84.10×(1−7%) = ₹16,041,486. NPV = ₹16,041,486×4.623−₹9,391,000=₹64,766,861. Decision: Accept.
487Real OptionsReal options case: Static NPV ₹-2,190,987; option to defer ₹176,100; option to expand ₹269,150; option to abandon ₹146,750. Find expanded NPV.Expanded NPV = static NPV + option values = ₹-1,598,987. Decision: Reject unless strategic reasons dominate.
488Social CBASocial CBA case: Private NPV ₹-1,761,711; PV of social benefits ₹578,000; PV of social costs ₹254,600. Compute social NPV.Social NPV = ₹-1,761,711+₹578,000−₹254,600=₹-1,438,311. Social decision: Reject/redesign.
489WACC/CAPMWACC/CAPM case: Rf 6%, market return 13%, project beta 1.1, pre-tax debt cost 12%, tax 30%, debt weight 30%. Estimate project WACC.Ke = 6% + 1.1×(13%−6%) = 13.70%. After-tax Kd = 8.40%. WACC = 70%×Ke + 30%×Kd(1−T) = 12.11%.
490Economic LifeEconomic life case: Asset cost ₹9,465,000; operating cost rises every year; salvage value falls every year; discount rate 12%. Explain how to choose replacement year.Compute PV total cost for each possible life: initial cost + PV operating costs − PV salvage. Convert each to EAC = PV cost/PVAF. Choose the year with minimum EAC.
491Inflation AdjustmentInflation case: Real annual CF ₹1,445,250; real discount rate 8%; inflation 9%; life 4; initial investment ₹9,483,500. Find nominal discount rate and real-method NPV.Nominal rate = (1+8%)(1+9%)−1 = 17.72%. Real-method NPV = ₹-4,696,649. Use nominal cash flows only with nominal rate.
492Working CapitalWorking capital case: Initial asset investment ₹9,502,000; working capital ₹1,140,240; annual CF ₹1,448,000; WC recovered at end; life 5; rate 14%. Compute NPV.Year-0 outflow = asset + WC = ₹10,642,240. PV inflows = ₹4,971,101; PV WC recovery = ₹592,205. NPV = ₹-5,078,934. Decision: Reject.
493Depreciation Tax ShieldDepreciation shield case: Asset cost ₹9,520,500; life 6; straight-line depreciation; tax rate 30%; discount rate 15%. Compute annual and PV tax shield.Annual depreciation = ₹1,586,750. Annual tax shield = ₹476,025. PV tax shield = ₹476,025×3.784=₹1,801,508.
494APVAPV case: Base-case NPV ₹-3,668,945; debt raised ₹4,769,500; corporate tax 30%; issue costs ₹190,780. Estimate APV using perpetual debt tax shield.PV debt tax shield = Debt×T = ₹1,430,850. APV = base NPV + tax shield − issue cost = ₹-2,428,875. Decision: Reject.
495Decision TreeDecision tree case: Stage-1 cost ₹1,433,625; success probability 0.70. If successful, invest ₹6,212,375; high PV ₹14,336,250 probability 0.6; low PV ₹5,256,625. Find rollback NPV.Stage-2 NPV = 0.6×₹14,336,250+0.4×₹5,256,625−₹6,212,375=₹4,492,025. Overall NPV = 0.70×max(Stage-2 NPV,0)−₹1,433,625=₹1,710,793. Decision: Proceed.
496SensitivitySensitivity case: Base project has initial investment ₹9,576,000, annual CF ₹1,459,000, life 9, rate 9%. Test NPV if annual CF falls/rises by 10%.Base NPV = ₹-828,935. Downside NPV = ₹-1,703,641. Upside NPV = ₹45,772. If downside becomes negative, project is cash-flow sensitive.
497Scenario AnalysisScenario case: Initial investment ₹9,594,500; life 3; rate 10%. Worst/base/best annual CFs are ₹1,096,312, ₹1,461,750, ₹1,827,188. Compute scenario NPVs.Worst NPV ₹-6,868,133; base NPV ₹-5,959,344; best NPV ₹-5,050,555. Interpret whether the range crosses zero.
498MIRRMIRR case: Investment ₹9,613,000; annual CF ₹1,464,500 for 4 years; reinvestment rate 11%. Compute MIRR.Terminal value of inflows = ₹6,897,401. MIRR = (TV/I)^(1/n)−1 = -7.96%. Compare with required return.
499Discounted PaybackDiscounted payback case: Investment ₹9,631,500; annual CF ₹1,467,250; rate 12%; life 5. Compute discounted payback.Cumulative discounted inflows by year 5 = ₹5,289,108; investment is not recovered within project life.
500Profitability IndexPI case: Investment ₹9,650,000; annual CF ₹1,470,000; life 6; discount rate 13%. Compute PI.PV inflows = ₹5,876,398. PI = PV inflows / investment = 0.609. Decision: Reject.

MCQMCQ 1: Which method directly measures addition to shareholder wealth? Options: Payback | ARR | NPV | Book valueNPV
MCQMCQ 2: Which cost is ignored because it has already been incurred? Options: Opportunity cost | Sunk cost | Incremental cost | Working capitalSunk cost
MCQMCQ 3: Working capital recovery at project end is treated as: Options: Cash inflow | Cash outflow | Depreciation | Financing costCash inflow
MCQMCQ 4: IRR is the rate at which: Options: PI is zero | NPV is zero | Payback is zero | ARR is maximumNPV is zero
MCQMCQ 5: MIRR assumes reinvestment at: Options: IRR | Accounting rate | Specified reinvestment rate | Zero rateSpecified reinvestment rate
MCQMCQ 6: For mutually exclusive projects with equal lives, the best primary rule is: Options: Highest NPV | Shortest payback | Highest ARR | Lowest outlayHighest NPV
MCQMCQ 7: Depreciation affects cash flow through: Options: Tax shield | Interest | Dividend | Market priceTax shield
