Level 1 · Core foundation

Capital Budgeting Basics A–Z

Capital budgeting is the process of evaluating long-term investments whose benefits and costs extend beyond one accounting period. It answers one main question: Should scarce long-term funds be committed to this project?

Meaning

Capital budgeting means planning, analysing, selecting, implementing and reviewing long-term investment projects such as plant, machinery, product lines, technology, acquisitions, infrastructure and major replacements.

Goal

The financial goal is to maximise shareholder wealth by accepting projects whose present value of benefits exceeds their present value of costs, subject to risk, strategy and capital constraints.

Why It Matters

Capital budgeting decisions involve large funds, long horizons, uncertain future cash flows, strategic consequences and often irreversible commitments.

Basic Vocabulary

TermMeaningDecision Use
Capital expenditureLong-term spending that creates future capacity or benefit.Needs formal approval and evaluation.
Operating expenditureDay-to-day expense consumed in the current period.Usually handled in operating budgets.
Cash flowActual cash inflow/outflow, not accounting profit.Primary input for DCF methods.
Initial outlayCash committed at time zero.Usually negative cash flow.
Terminal cash flowFinal-year cash flow including salvage and working capital recovery.Often materially affects NPV.
Discount rateRequired return reflecting time value and risk.Used to convert future cash flows to present value.
Independent projectAcceptance does not affect other projects.Accept if NPV is positive.
Mutually exclusive projectOnly one alternative can be selected.Choose higher NPV or EAC for unequal lives.

Beginner Decision Rule

If NPV > 0: project adds value → Accept. If NPV = 0: project earns exactly required return → Indifferent / accept for strategic reasons. If NPV < 0: project destroys value → Reject. For mutually exclusive projects: choose the alternative that adds the most value, not necessarily the highest percentage return.
Level 1 · Mathematical foundation

Time Value of Money and Discounting

A rupee today is worth more than a rupee in the future because money can earn a return and future cash flows are risky. Capital budgeting depends on converting cash flows across time into comparable present values.

TVM Calculator

Dashboard

Future value of PV—
Present value of FV—
PV factor—
FV factor—

Core Formulas

Future Value: FV = PV × (1+r)^n Present Value: PV = FV / (1+r)^n Present Value Factor: PVF = 1 / (1+r)^n Present Value Annuity Factor: PVAF = [1 − (1+r)^−n] / r

Exam Notes

  • Use year 0 for initial outlay and no discounting at time 0.
  • Discount year 1 cash flow by one period, year 2 by two periods, etc.
  • Use nominal rate with nominal cash flows; real rate with real cash flows.
  • Do not compare raw cash totals across different years.
Level 1–2 · Before calculations

Project Identification, Screening and Capital Budget Request

Good capital budgeting starts before NPV. Firms need a pipeline of proposals, screening criteria, approval limits and documentation standards.

Sources of Project Ideas

  • Cost reduction or automation
  • Capacity expansion
  • New products or markets
  • Replacement and modernisation
  • Regulatory or safety compliance
  • Environmental improvements
  • Research and development
  • Mergers, acquisitions and strategic partnerships

Initial Screening Tests

  • Strategic fit with business plan
  • Legal/regulatory feasibility
  • Technical feasibility
  • Minimum expected return
  • Budget availability
  • Risk class and uncertainty
  • Operational capability
  • ESG and reputation impact

Capital Expenditure Request Template

SectionWhat to Include
Project summaryPurpose, sponsor, location, expected start and completion dates.
Strategic rationaleProblem solved, opportunity captured, connection to strategy.
Financial caseInitial outlay, cash flows, NPV, IRR, payback, sensitivity.
Risk assessmentKey assumptions, downside scenarios, mitigation plan.
Implementation planMilestones, vendors, responsibilities, control process.
Post-audit planWhen actual results will be compared to forecasts.
Important: Weak proposals should be filtered out early. Full DCF analysis should be reserved for projects that pass strategic, technical and compliance screening.
Level 2 · Building reliable inputs

Forecasting Assumptions for Capital Budgeting

The accuracy of NPV depends more on forecast quality than formula complexity. Forecasting should identify volume, price, cost, working capital, tax, inflation and terminal assumptions explicitly.

Revenue Forecast

  • Market size and growth
  • Market share
  • Selling price and price erosion
  • Ramp-up period
  • Seasonality and capacity limits
  • Cannibalisation of existing sales

Cost Forecast

  • Variable cost per unit
  • Fixed operating cost
  • Maintenance and downtime
  • Energy and labour escalation
  • Learning curve effects
  • Supplier risk and logistics cost

Balance-Sheet Forecast

  • Inventory days
  • Receivable days
  • Payable days
  • Spare parts and safety stock
  • Working capital release
  • Residual value and disposal costs

Forecast Quality Checklist

Traceable

Every number should link to a source: market study, vendor quote, engineering estimate, historical data or management assumption.

Consistent

Volumes must match capacity; inflation must match discount rate; tax assumptions must match jurisdiction.

Tested

Run sensitivity and scenario analysis on the few variables that drive most of the NPV.

Level 2–3 · Mutually exclusive decisions

Project Ranking, NPV Profile and Crossover Rate

When projects are mutually exclusive, rankings can differ across NPV, IRR, PI and payback. The crossover rate is the discount rate at which two projects have the same NPV. Below that rate one project may dominate; above it the ranking can reverse.

Project A

Project B

Evaluation Rate

Ranking Dashboard

NPV A—
NPV B—
Crossover rate—
NPV-preferred—

Ranking Rules

Independent projects: accept all positive-NPV projects if capital is available. Mutually exclusive, same life: choose highest NPV at the appropriate discount rate. Mutually exclusive, unequal life: use Equivalent Annual Cost/Benefit or replacement chain. Capital rationing: maximise total NPV of the package within the budget.
Level 3 · Project-specific discount rate

Project Beta and CAPM-Based Required Return

When a project has risk different from the firm's average risk, using company WACC can be misleading. A project-specific required return can be estimated using CAPM and comparable-company beta.

CAPM Calculator

Dashboard

Market risk premium—
Cost of equity—
After-tax cost of debt—
Project WACC—

Formula

CAPM Cost of Equity: Ke = Rf + β × (Rm − Rf) Project WACC = Equity weight × Ke + Debt weight × Kd × (1 − Tax) Use comparable-company asset beta when the project's business risk differs from the existing firm.
Level 3 · Public sector and ESG-heavy projects

Social Cost-Benefit Analysis

Some projects, especially infrastructure, public sector, environmental and development projects, must be evaluated not only by private cash flows but also by social costs and benefits. These may include employment, pollution, time savings, safety, health and regional development.

Social NPV Calculator

Dashboard

Net social value—
Weighted social value—
Total adjusted NPV—
Decision—

Examples of Social Benefits and Costs

Benefits

Travel time saved, reduced emissions, safer workplaces, employment, skill creation, regional development.

Costs

Pollution, displacement, congestion, ecological damage, public health risk, loss of community assets.

Method

Quantify where possible using shadow prices; disclose non-quantified effects separately.

Level 3–4 · Advanced uncertainty analysis

Advanced Risk Toolkit

Advanced capital budgeting does not rely on a single forecast. It analyses the distribution of outcomes, the variables that matter most, and the managerial actions available when reality differs from the forecast.

Risk Techniques and When to Use Them

TechniqueBest Used When
Sensitivity analysisYou need to identify key value drivers one at a time.
Scenario analysisYou need coherent best/base/worst cases.
Break-even analysisYou need minimum volume/price/cost condition for NPV ≥ 0.
Decision treeInvestment is staged and probabilities are available.
Monte Carlo simulationMany uncertain variables interact.
Certainty equivalentRisk differs by year or cash-flow component.
RADR / CAPMRisk is captured through the discount rate.
Real optionsManagement can defer, expand, abandon or switch.

Break-Even Annual Cash Flow for NPV = 0

PVAF—
Break-even annual CF—

Advanced Risk Principle

Risk analysis should answer: 1. What variables drive NPV the most? 2. What is the probability of value destruction? 3. What managerial choices exist if the downside appears? 4. Is the risk diversifiable, systematic, operational, financial, regulatory or strategic?
Level 4 · Managerial reality

Capital Budgeting Governance and Behavioural Biases

Even technically correct models can lead to poor decisions if governance is weak or human biases distort forecasts. Advanced capital budgeting requires process discipline.

Common Behavioural Biases

  • Optimism bias: overestimating revenue and underestimating cost.
  • Escalation of commitment: continuing a failing project because money was already spent.
  • Anchoring: relying too heavily on an initial estimate.
  • Strategic misrepresentation: deliberately optimistic forecasts to get approval.
  • Confirmation bias: selecting evidence that supports the sponsor's preferred project.
  • Availability bias: overweighting recent success/failure stories.

Governance Controls

  • Independent review of large project forecasts
  • Standard templates and assumption registers
  • Stage-gate approval for risky projects
  • Clear authority limits by project size/risk
  • Mandatory sensitivity and scenario analysis
  • Post-audit feedback linked to future approvals
  • Separation between project sponsor and approval committee
  • Contingency budgets and change-control process

Stage-Gate Model

Idea→Pre-feasibility→Detailed business case→Investment committee→Execution gate→Post-audit

Final Integrated Rule

A complete capital budgeting answer should identify the decision type, build relevant post-tax cash flows, apply a risk-appropriate discount rate, compute NPV and supporting criteria, analyse risk and constraints, consider strategic/ESG/governance issues, and recommend a clear action.

Recommended Full Decision Sequence

Define project→Estimate incremental post-tax cash flows→Choose WACC / required return→Compute NPV and support metrics→Stress-test risk→Check constraints and strategy→Approve, implement, audit

Use NPV as the main wealth-maximisation criterion; use other methods as supporting diagnostics rather than substitutes for NPV.

Cost of Capital and WACC in Capital Budgeting

The discount rate used in NPV is usually the project-specific opportunity cost of capital. For a project with risk similar to the firm's existing operations and financed in target proportions, the common benchmark is Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC). For projects with different risk, WACC must be adjusted or replaced by a project-specific required return.

WACC Calculator

Dashboard

Equity weight—
Debt weight—
After-tax cost of debt—
Base WACC—
Project-specific rate—

Formula and Use

WACC = [E / (D+E)] × Ke + [D / (D+E)] × Kd × (1 − Tax Rate) Project-specific discount rate = WACC ± risk adjustment Use WACC only when the project has similar business risk and target capital structure.

Relevant / Incremental Cash Flow Rules

Capital budgeting should include only cash flows that change because the project is accepted. Accounting profit is not enough; financing charges are excluded, sunk costs are ignored, opportunity costs are included, and all figures should be post-tax.

Include in Project Cash Flows

  • Initial capital outlay and installation costs
  • Incremental sales and cost savings
  • Incremental operating costs
  • Opportunity cost of assets used
  • Working capital investment and later recovery
  • Depreciation tax shield
  • After-tax salvage value
  • Cannibalisation of existing product contribution
  • Incremental overheads caused by the project

Exclude from Project Cash Flows

  • Sunk costs already incurred
  • Allocated overheads that do not increase
  • Interest on debt and dividends
  • Book profit not converted to cash flow
  • Non-incremental shared expenses
  • Historical purchase price of assets if current opportunity value is different

Depreciation Methods and Tax Shields

Depreciation is not a cash outflow, but it changes taxable income and therefore creates a tax shield. Different depreciation methods change the timing of tax shields; faster depreciation usually increases NPV because tax savings arrive earlier.

Compare Methods

Tax-Shield Comparison

PV shield — Straight line—
PV shield — WDV—
Better method by PV—

Key Point

Depreciation Tax Shield in year t = Depreciation(t) × Tax Rate PV of Tax Shield = Σ [Depreciation(t) × Tax Rate] / (1+r)^t Accelerated methods improve NPV when they move tax shields into earlier years.

Terminal Value, Salvage Value and Disposal Tax

The final year's project cash flow often includes more than operating cash flow: salvage proceeds, tax on gain or loss, dismantling costs, site restoration costs, and recovery of working capital. Missing terminal adjustments is one of the most common capital budgeting errors.

Terminal Cash Flow Calculator

Dashboard

Taxable gain / loss—
Tax on disposal—
After-tax salvage—
Total terminal CF—
Terminal CF = Final-year operating CFAT + Sale Proceeds − Tax on Gain + Tax Saving on Loss − Dismantling/Restoration Costs + Working Capital Recovery

Lease vs Buy Decision

A lease-versus-buy decision is a financing-form comparison for acquiring the same asset. The operating benefits of the asset are usually identical under both alternatives, so the analysis compares the present value of after-tax costs under buying versus leasing.

Inputs

PV Cost Comparison

PV cost of buying—
PV cost of leasing—
Preferred option—

International Capital Budgeting

International projects add foreign exchange risk, country risk, blocked funds, remittance restrictions, different inflation rates, withholding taxes, and political/regulatory uncertainty. The correct rule is consistency: estimate cash flows in one currency and discount at a matching currency-specific required return, or convert expected foreign cash flows into home currency using expected exchange rates.

Foreign Project NPV

Dashboard

PV of remitted cash flows—
Home-currency NPV—
Decision—

International Checklist

Currency

Forecast exchange rates, inflation differential, remittance currency and hedging policy.

Tax

Local tax, withholding tax, home-country tax credits and transfer pricing.

Risk

Political risk, expropriation, blocked funds, regulatory approvals, environmental and labour compliance.

Real Options in Capital Budgeting

Traditional NPV assumes a fixed plan. Real options recognise that managers can respond to new information: defer investment, expand if demand is strong, abandon if results are poor, switch inputs/outputs, or stage the project. These options can make a project more valuable than its static NPV.

Main Real Options

  • Option to defer — wait before committing capital.
  • Option to expand — invest more if early results are favourable.
  • Option to abandon — stop the project and recover salvage value if performance is weak.
  • Option to switch — change input mix, output mix, location or technology.
  • Option to stage — invest sequentially rather than all at once.

Strategic NPV Adjuster

Expanded strategic NPV—
Decision—

Formula

Expanded NPV = Static NPV + Value of managerial flexibility / real options Accept if Expanded NPV ≥ 0, but document assumptions behind option values carefully.

ESG, Strategic and Qualitative Factors

Not every important effect can be captured perfectly in forecast cash flows. Capital budgeting committees should explicitly document qualitative considerations alongside the numerical NPV.

Strategic Fit

  • Alignment with corporate strategy
  • Competitive advantage and entry barriers
  • Technology roadmap and scalability
  • Customer experience and brand impact
  • Supply-chain resilience

ESG and Social Factors

  • Carbon emissions and energy efficiency
  • Water use, waste, biodiversity
  • Worker safety and labour standards
  • Community impact and licence to operate
  • Regulatory compliance and future carbon pricing

Governance Factors

  • Approval authority and accountability
  • Ethical sourcing and anti-corruption risk
  • Data privacy and cybersecurity
  • Permits, legal exposure and litigation risk
  • Post-audit transparency
Practical rule: If a qualitative factor is material and measurable, convert it into cash flows or a risk-adjustment. If it is material but not reliably measurable, disclose it separately and make the decision committee explicitly sign off on the judgement.

Implementation, Control and Post-Completion Audit

Capital budgeting does not end with approval. Large projects require implementation control, milestone monitoring, variance analysis and post-completion audit to improve future forecasting discipline.

Implementation Control

Approval note→Capital sanction→Procurement→Milestones→Commissioning
  • Budgeted vs actual capital expenditure
  • Time overruns and cost escalation
  • Change orders and scope creep
  • Safety, quality and compliance checks

Post-Audit Questions

  1. Were actual cash flows close to forecasts?
  2. Were tax shields, working capital and terminal values estimated correctly?
  3. Did the project deliver strategic benefits promised?
  4. What caused variance: price, volume, timing, execution, macro factors?
  5. Should forecast models or approval thresholds be changed?

Post-Audit Table Template

ItemForecastActualVarianceReasonAction
Capital costBudgetActual spendOver/underSupplier, design, delayImprove estimation/controls
Revenue/cost savingsForecast CFActual CFFavourable/unfavourableDemand, price, efficiencyUpdate assumptions
Working capitalPlannedActualVarianceInventory/credit termsTighten policies
Strategic outcomeBusiness caseObservedGapMarket/competitionReview strategy

Economic Life and Replacement Timing

An asset's best replacement date is often not its physical life. The economic life is the period that minimises equivalent annual cost or maximises equivalent annual benefit, considering purchase cost, operating cost, maintenance, downtime and salvage value.

Economic Life Calculator

EAC by Replacement Year

Best replacement year—
Minimum equivalent annual cost—
PV Cost if replaced at year n = Initial Cost + PV(Operating Costs through n) − PV(Salvage at n) Equivalent Annual Cost = PV Cost / PVAF(r,n) Choose the year with the lowest EAC.

Exam Framework and Common Mistakes

Use this checklist when solving any capital budgeting practical problem.

Universal Solving Framework

  1. Identify whether the problem is independent, mutually exclusive, replacement, rationing, lease-buy, international or unequal-life.
  2. Build a time line from year 0 to terminal year.
  3. Separate initial outflow, annual operating cash flows and terminal cash flow.
  4. Exclude sunk costs and financing costs.
  5. Include opportunity costs, working capital, tax shields and after-tax salvage.
  6. Choose the correct discount rate.
  7. Compute NPV first, then PI/IRR/MIRR/payback as supporting measures.
  8. For mutually exclusive projects, prefer the higher NPV/EAC answer depending on equal/unequal lives.
  9. Stress-test with sensitivity/scenario/risk methods.
  10. State a clear decision and reason.

Common Mistakes

  • Adding depreciation as a cash inflow without first computing tax properly.
  • Deducting interest in project cash flows and also discounting at WACC.
  • Ignoring working capital recovery at the end.
  • Using book value instead of opportunity value for an existing asset.
  • Forgetting tax on sale of old/new assets.
  • Choosing IRR over NPV for mutually exclusive projects with scale/timing differences.
  • Mixing real cash flows with nominal discount rates.
  • Using PI ranking under indivisible capital rationing without checking combinations.
  • Comparing unequal-life projects by raw NPV only.
  • Ignoring strategic, ESG or regulatory constraints after numerical approval.

One-Line Rule

Capital budgeting is not just formula substitution; it is a disciplined process for converting a strategic investment idea into incremental post-tax cash flows, discounting them at the right required return, and choosing the alternative that maximises present wealth after risk and constraints.

How to Read the Solver

Do the criteria agree?

If NPV is positive, PI is above 1, and IRR/MIRR exceed the discount rate, every technique points the same way — a straightforward accept.

Where do they typically disagree?

Scale, timing, or unequal-life differences between mutually exclusive projects, or a fast payback masking a mediocre IRR.

Which one should decide?

NPV is the criterion that stays consistent with shareholder wealth maximisation whenever the others conflict.

Scenario Analysis

NPV Sensitivity Lab

Capital budgeting decisions rest on two shaky estimates — the discount rate and the cash-flow forecast. This matrix shows how much the NPV verdict itself can move when either assumption is off.

NPV Matrix — Discount Rate × Cash-Flow Scenario

Why Sensitivity Matters

NPV is non-linear in both the discount rate and the horizon — a project that looks comfortably positive at the base case can turn negative with a modest downward revision to cash flows or a modest rise in the required return. Running this kind of matrix before committing capital is standard practice, and is exactly what the earlier discussion of scale, timing and life disparities is warning against relying on a single point estimate.

Two Families of Technique in This Lab

The core appraisal techniques (Payback through APV) all answer "is this project worth doing, given its forecast cash flows?" The risk-analysis techniques added here answer a different, complementary question: "how much confidence should I place in that forecast, and how does the answer change if it's wrong?" A mature capital budgeting process uses both — a technique like NPV to make the accept/reject call, and a risk technique like sensitivity, scenario, or simulation analysis to stress-test that call before committing capital.

How Every Technique Connects Back to NPV

Every discounted technique here — PI, IRR, Discounted Payback, MIRR — is built on the same present-value engine as NPV; they simply repackage the same discounted cash flows into a ratio, a rate, a break-even year, or a terminal-value-adjusted rate. When techniques disagree, it's because they're answering subtly different questions (a rate versus a rupee amount, for instance) — not because one of them is "wrong." NPV is the one that answers the actual decision question — does this add wealth — directly.

Reference

Complete Formula Sheet

Payback Period Uniform: Investment / Annual Cash Inflow Non-uniform: Year cumulative CF reaches investment, + fraction
Payback Reciprocal Average Annual Cash Inflow / Initial Investment
Accounting Rate of Return Average Annual Net Income / Investment (initial or average) Average Investment = ½(Initial − Salvage) + Salvage + Addl. WC
Net Present Value NPV = Σ Cₜ/(1+k)ᵗ − I
Profitability Index PI = Σ PV(Cash Inflows) / Initial Outlay
Internal Rate of Return IRR = LR + [NPV at LR / (NPV at LR − NPV at HR)] × (HR − LR)
Discounted Payback Same as Payback, but cash flows are discounted before accumulating
Modified IRR TV = Σ CFₜ×(1+r)^(n−t) MIRR = (TV / Investment)^(1/n) − 1
Depreciation Tax Shield Tax Shield = Depreciation × Tax Rate
Exclusion of Financing Costs PAT excl. financing cost = PBIT × (1 − Tax Rate)
Cash Inflow After Tax (CFAT) CFAT = (Contribution − Fixed Cost − Depreciation)×(1−Tax) + Depreciation
Capital Rationing (Divisible) Rank by NPV per ₹1 invested = NPV / Investment
Equivalent Annualised Criterion PVAF(r,n) = [1−(1+r)⁻ⁿ]/r EAC = NPV / PVAF
Adjusted Present Value APV = Base-Case NPV − Issue Costs + PV of Tax Relief on Debt
Risk-Adjusted Discount Rate RADR = Risk-Free Rate + Risk Premium NPV = Σ CFt/(1+RADR)^t − I
Certainty Equivalent Method NPV = Σ [CFt × αt]/(1+Rf)^t − I
Expected NPV E(NPV) = Σ [Probability(i) × NPV(i)]
Standard Deviation & Coefficient of Variation σ = √Σ[Probability(i) × (NPV(i) − E(NPV))²] CV = σ / E(NPV)
Decision Tree (Roll-Back) EV(node) = Σ [Probability(branch) × Value(branch)] Solve right-to-left; at each decision node take max(invest, abandon)
Replacement Analysis Incremental Outflow = New Asset Cost − Old Sale Value − Tax Effect Tax Effect = (Book Value − Sale Value) × Tax Rate
Fisher Equation (Inflation) (1+Nominal) = (1+Real) × (1+Inflation)

Glossary

Capital Budgeting

Applying the principles of budgeting to long-term capital investment decisions.

Incremental Cash Flow

The change in the firm's total cash flow that results directly from accepting a project.

Sunk Cost

Cash already spent and irreversible — excluded from the decision entirely.

Opportunity Cost

The benefit foregone by using a resource on this project instead of its next-best alternative.

Discount Rate / Cut-off Rate

The minimum required return, typically the firm's WACC, used to discount project cash flows.

Terminal Value (in MIRR)

The future value of all interim cash flows, reinvested at a stated rate through to the project's final year.

Mutually Exclusive Projects

Accepting one automatically means rejecting the other(s).

Capital Rationing

A capital budget constraint that forces a choice among positive-NPV projects.

Block of Assets

A group of assets of the same class, depreciated together at the same rate under tax law.

Certainty Equivalent Coefficient

A factor (0 to 1) that converts a risky expected cash flow into the smaller, certain amount considered equally desirable.

Coefficient of Variation

Standard deviation of NPV divided by expected NPV — a scale-free measure of risk, useful for comparing projects of different sizes.

Decision Tree

A diagram of sequential decisions and chance events, solved by rolling back from the final branch to the first decision.

Monte Carlo Simulation

Repeated random sampling of uncertain inputs to build a full probability distribution of possible project outcomes.

Real vs. Nominal

Real values are expressed in constant (inflation-free) purchasing power; nominal values include the effect of inflation. Never mix the two.

Incremental Analysis

Evaluating a decision (such as a replacement) only on the basis of what changes versus the next-best alternative.

Core Decision Rule

Whenever techniques disagree on a mutually exclusive choice, NPV is the criterion in conformity with the wealth-maximisation objective — it directly measures the rupee addition to shareholder wealth, while Payback, ARR, PI and IRR each answer a related but distinct question (speed of recovery, accounting return, capital efficiency, and implied rate of return, respectively).

Payback & ARR

Excel: Payback (uniform): =Investment/AnnualCashFlow ARR: =AverageProfit/Investment R: payback <- function(inv,cf) inv/cf arr <- function(avgProfit,investment) avgProfit/investment

NPV & PI

Excel: =NPV(rate, cashflow_range) + initial_outflow (initial outflow entered as a negative number separately, at time 0) PI: =NPV(rate,cashflow_range)/-InitialOutlay R: npv <- function(rate,cfs) sum(cfs/(1+rate)^seq_along(cfs)) pi <- function(pv_inflows,outlay) pv_inflows/outlay

IRR & MIRR

Excel: =IRR(cashflow_range_including_outflow) =MIRR(cashflow_range, finance_rate, reinvest_rate) R: irr <- function(cfs){ # cfs[1] is the negative initial outflow f <- function(r) sum(cfs/(1+r)^(seq_along(cfs)-1)) uniroot(f, c(-0.99,5))$root } mirr <- function(outflow,inflows,reinvest){ n <- length(inflows) tv <- sum(inflows*(1+reinvest)^(n-seq_along(inflows))) (tv/outflow)^(1/n)-1 }

Discounted Payback

Excel: build a discounted-cash-flow column, then a cumulative column, and read off where cumulative crosses the initial investment (interpolate the fraction). R: disc_payback <- function(investment,cfs,rate){ disc <- cfs/(1+rate)^seq_along(cfs) cum <- cumsum(disc) yr <- which(cum >= investment)[1] prevcum <- if(yr>1) cum[yr-1] else 0 (yr-1) + (investment-prevcum)/disc[yr] }

Capital Rationing (Indivisible, Brute Force)

Excel: use Solver with a binary (0/1) decision variable per project, maximizing Σ(NPV_i × x_i) subject to Σ(Investment_i × x_i) ≤ Budget. R: best_combo <- function(invest,npv,budget){ n <- length(invest); best <- -Inf; bestset <- c() for(mask in 0:(2^n-1)){ idx <- which(bitwAnd(mask, 2^(0:(n-1))) > 0) if(sum(invest[idx]) <= budget && sum(npv[idx]) > best){ best <- sum(npv[idx]); bestset <- idx } } list(npv=best, projects=bestset) }

Equivalent Annualised Criterion & APV

Excel: PVAF: =(1-(1+rate)^-years)/rate EAC: =NPV/PVAF APV: =BaseNPV - IssueCosts + (AmountRaised*DebtRate*Tax)/DebtRate R: pvaf <- function(r,n) (1-(1+r)^-n)/r eac <- function(npv,r,n) npv/pvaf(r,n) apv <- function(basenpv,issuecost,amtraised,debtrate,tax) basenpv - issuecost + (amtraised*debtrate*tax)/debtrate

Risk Analysis — RADR, Certainty Equivalent & Expected NPV

Excel: RADR NPV: =NPV(RiskFreeRate+RiskPremium,CashFlowRange)+Outflow Certainty Equiv: =NPV(RiskFreeRate,CFRange*CoeffRange)+Outflow [array formula] Expected NPV: =SUMPRODUCT(Probabilities,ScenarioNPVs) R: radr_npv <- function(cfs,rf,premium,invest) sum(cfs/(1+rf+premium)^seq_along(cfs))-invest expected_npv <- function(probs,npvs) sum(probs*npvs)

Risk Measurement — Standard Deviation & Simulation

Excel: Std Dev: =SQRT(SUMPRODUCT(Probabilities,(NPVs-ExpectedNPV)^2)) Coeff Var: =StdDev/ExpectedNPV Simulation: use Data Table or =NORM.INV(RAND(),Mean,StdDev) per trial, then AVERAGE/STDEV across trials R: cv <- function(probs,npvs){ e <- sum(probs*npvs) sd <- sqrt(sum(probs*(npvs-e)^2)) sd/e } simulate_npv <- function(trials,years,mean,sd,rate,invest){ replicate(trials, sum(rnorm(years,mean,sd)/(1+rate)^(1:years))-invest) }

Decision Tree & Replacement Analysis

Excel: Decision Tree (roll-back), build right to left: Stage2EV: =SUMPRODUCT(Probabilities,PVs) Stage2NPV: =Stage2EV-Stage2Cost Stage1EV: =ProbSuccess*MAX(Stage2NPV,0)+((1-ProbSuccess)*FailValue) Replacement: =NewCost-OldSaleValue-((OldBookValue-OldSaleValue)*TaxRate) R: replacement_outflow <- function(newCost,oldSale,oldBook,tax) newCost-oldSale-((oldBook-oldSale)*tax)

Inflation Adjustment (Fisher Equation)

Excel: NominalRate: =(1+RealRate)*(1+Inflation)-1 NominalCF: =RealCF*(1+Inflation)^Year R: nominal_rate <- function(real,inflation) (1+real)*(1+inflation)-1 nominal_cf <- function(realCF,inflation,t) realCF*(1+inflation)^t

Recommended Spreadsheet Layout for Any DCF Technique

RowContent
1Period 0, 1, 2, … n across columns
2Cash flow in each period (year 0 = negative initial outflow)
3Discount factor = 1/(1+rate)^period
4Present value = cash flow × discount factor
5Running cumulative PV (for payback / discounted payback)
6Sum of row 4 = NPV; NPV/|row-0 outflow| = PI; =IRR(row 2) = IRR

Building every technique off this single row layout — rather than separate ad-hoc calculations — is what lets Payback, NPV, PI and IRR all be read off the same worksheet, exactly as the Master Capital Budgeting Solver does in this lab.

Practice Lab

Work each problem, then reveal the solution to check your method. Drawn from classic worked illustrations and practical problems.

Teacher Mode

Learning Objectives

  • State the objectives of capital investment decisions.
  • Discuss the importance and purpose of capital budgeting.
  • Calculate cash flows in capital budgeting decisions and explain the basic principles for measuring them.
  • Discuss and apply Payback Period, ARR, NPV, PI, IRR, Discounted Payback Period, and MIRR.
  • Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each evaluation technique.

Classroom Activities

  1. Walk through the tax-shield-from-depreciation example live, contrasting cash flow with and without depreciation, before moving to the block-of-assets nuances.
  2. Give students the same project data and have them compute Payback, ARR, NPV, PI and IRR separately, then compare rankings — this reliably surfaces the conflict scenarios covered earlier.
  3. Reproduce Illustration 10 (scale disparity) live using the NPV vs IRR Conflicts module, then vary the discount rate to show how the crossover rate changes the conclusion.
  4. Run a capital-rationing exercise with 5–6 projects and a fixed budget; have students first rank by NPV-per-rupee assuming divisibility, then challenge them to find the better indivisible combination by hand before revealing the brute-force answer.
  5. Have students solve an IRR by trial-and-error/interpolation by hand once, then use the calculator to confirm — this builds intuition for why the interpolation formula works.

Exam Question Bank — By Section

Conceptual

Classify the types of capital investment decisions on both bases discussed in this lab, with an example of each.

Explain the exclusion of financing costs principle and why it prevents double-counting the cost of capital.

Numerical

Given a project's cash flows, compute Payback, ARR, NPV, PI and IRR, and identify any ranking conflicts.

Given two mutually exclusive projects of very different scale, demonstrate the scale-disparity conflict between NPV and IRR.

Applied / Case

Given a capital-constrained budget and several positive-NPV projects, determine the optimal package under both the divisible and indivisible assumptions.

Given two projects with unequal lives, apply the Equivalent Annualised Criterion to select the better one.

Sample Practical Problem

Following data has been made available for a capital project:

Annual cash inflows₹1,00,000
Useful life4 years
Salvage value0
Internal rate of return12%
Profitability index1.064

You are required to calculate: (i) Cost of project, (ii) Cost of capital, (iii) Net present value, (iv) Payback period. (PV factors at 9%–12% are provided in the original text.) Try backing out the cost of project from the PI and IRR given, using the NPV and IRR calculators in this lab to check your work.
